title: Profound Autism Prevalence and Assessment Practices in a Population-Based Study
journal: J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Profound autism is a proposed subcategory of autism including individuals unable to meet basic daily adaptive needs and requiring 24-hour care. This report describes documented assessment practices and profound autism prevalence derived using different definitions.

METHOD: Among 7,084 8-year-old children with autism from a population-based surveillance program in 13 US sites in 2022, we calculated the availability of IQ, verbal status, and adaptive data. We imputed missing data to calculate profound autism prevalence using the "updated" (2025) definition, which includes having 1) either an intellectual quotient (IQ) score <50 OR being nonverbal/minimally verbal AND 2) adaptive functioning significantly below age level (≤70). We compared prevalence using the updated definition to using the "prior" (2021) profound autism definition that did not incorporate adaptive scores, the updated definition with higher IQ score cutoff (≤70), and using only nonverbal/minimally verbal status and adaptive ≤70.

RESULTS: Among children with autism, 61.1% had IQ data, 74.0% had verbal status data, and 55.9% had adaptive data available. Cognitive data (IQ or verbal status) and adaptive data were available to determine profound autism status for 54.4%. After imputation, updated definition profound autism prevalence was 5.4 (95% CI: 5.1-5.8) and nonprofound autism prevalence was 27.5 (95% CI: 26.8-28.1) per 1,000 8-year-olds in 2022. Of children with autism, 16.5% met the updated profound autism definition and 32.1% met one element of the definition but did not meet full criteria. Prevalence was 33.5% higher using the prior definition, 70.9% higher using the updated definition with higher IQ score cutoff, and 33.3% lower using only nonverbal/minimally verbal status and adaptive ≤70.

CONCLUSION: Prevalence of nonprofound autism was higher than profound autism. Adaptive or other assessments underlying the profound autism definition were missing almost half the time. Community evaluation practices and the profound autism definition can evolve to better understand and meet needs of individuals with autism.

title: Brain network localization of gray matter alterations and executive dysfunction in pediatric ADHD
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is characterized by gray matter alterations and executive dysfunction. Whether the spatially distributed regional abnormalities reported in previous meta-analyses converge within large-scale networks of the developing brain remains unclear. Using coordinate-informed functional connectivity network mapping (FCNM), we mapped the network architecture of meta-analytic gray matter volume (GMV) and executive dysfunction coordinates in pediatric ADHD and evaluated its reproducibility and cross-disorder specificity.

METHODS: We extracted neuroimaging coordinates from published meta-analyses reporting GMV alterations and task-based executive dysfunction in pediatric ADHD (n cases  = 5,015, n controls  = 5,915). To map these disparate regional coordinates onto common functional circuits, we applied FCNM utilizing a large-scale, high-quality pediatric normative connectome from the Chinese Child Brain Development (CCBD) project (n = 2,120). The spatial overlap between the derived abnormality networks and canonical brain networks was quantified using Dice coefficients. Furthermore, network robustness was validated using independent pediatric clinical cohorts (from the ADHD-200 dataset and CCBD), and disease specificity was assessed via cross-disorder connectomic comparison with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).

RESULTS: Despite the spatial dispersion of the input coordinates, the FCNM-derived connectivity maps showed differential overlap with large-scale brain networks. Specifically, the network associated with gray matter alterations localized predominantly to the default mode network (DMN) (Dice = 0.457; P NCT  = 0.001) and the ventral attention network (VAN) (Dice = 0.237; P NCT  = 0.03), while the network underlying executive dysfunction localized primarily to the VAN (Dice = 0.319; P NCT  = 0.001). Importantly, this dual-network architecture demonstrated robust reproducibility across independent clinical validation cohorts and exhibited clear topological specificity when compared to ASD-related networks.

CONCLUSIONS: Using a large pediatric normative connectome, coordinate-informed FCNM mapped ADHD-related abnormalities onto partially overlapping DMN and VAN architectures, providing a reproducible framework for understanding distributed abnormalities in ADHD and identifying biologically defined targets for neuromodulation and early intervention.

title: Change in the severity and impact of child psychiatric disorders over 3 years: an analysis of trends using the national child mental health surveys of England from 1999, 2004, and 2017
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Child and adolescent psychiatric disorders are common, now affecting at least one in eight children. Evidence points towards an increase in prevalence over time, but very few studies have tested whether longitudinal outcomes for children with mental health problems have changed. This study is the first to test whether mental health and functional outcomes for children with a diagnosed psychiatric disorder have improved or worsened across time in England.

METHODS: Three national probability surveys were undertaken in England in 1999, 2004, and 2017, each with respective 3-year follow-ups in 2002, 2007, and 2020. We include children at baseline aged 5-13 years and compare outcomes for those with baseline psychiatric diagnosis (mental health disorder or ADHD). Three-year mental health symptom severity and functional impairment were assessed using the parent- and self-rated total difficulties score and impact supplement from the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire.

RESULTS: Across all surveys, having a psychiatric disorder at baseline predicted greater difficulty and impact scores at follow-up. The magnitude of these associations increased sequentially over time, such that having a disorder at baseline was more strongly associated with parent- and self-rated difficulties in the 2017 survey compared with the 1999 and 2004 surveys. Children in the 2017 survey were also more likely to report a greater impact of problems. Patterns of individual change also showed a temporal gradient. For children with a psychiatric disorder in 1999, 34% experienced deterioration in mental health at the three-year follow-up, compared to 52% of those with a disorder in 2017. The proportion of those who improved decreased correspondingly.

CONCLUSIONS: Children with a psychiatric condition are experiencing increased difficulties in their daily lives compared to previous generations. Understanding why children are now more likely to experience impaired functioning is a major public concern.

title: Sex differences in the efficacy, acceptability, and tolerability of antipsychotics in people with acute schizophrenia: individual participant data pairwise, dose-response, and network meta-analyses
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Antipsychotics are the mainstay of schizophrenia treatment, but their efficacy and tolerability might differ between females and males, and previous evidence on sex differences has been inconsistent and methodologically limited. We aimed to evaluate sex differences in the efficacy, acceptability, and tolerability of antipsychotics in adults with acute schizophrenia.

METHODS: We performed individual participant data pairwise, dose-response, and network meta-analyses of antipsychotics versus placebo or another antipsychotic, using data from the Vivli and YODA trial data-sharing platforms (inception to April 9, 2025); the main analyses were restricted to fixed-dose trials. The primary outcome was overall symptoms on the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale at week 6 (or closest). Secondary outcomes included all-cause dropout and other efficacy and tolerability outcomes. We performed one-stage pairwise meta-analyses to quantitatively test sex-treatment interactions, and two-stage sex-stratified dose-response and network meta-analyses to visually examine potential sex differences. Credibility of effect modification was assessed with the Instrument to assess the Credibility of Effect Modification Analyses. People with lived experience were involved in planning and interpretation of the study. This study was registered with PROSPERO, CRD420251022957.

FINDINGS: We identified 33 eligible trials; 18 fixed-dose trials with 7062 participants (2168 females and 4894 males; of 5161 with race reported, 2954 White, 1187 Black, 752 Asian, and 268 of other or unspecified race; mean age 40·9 years; receiving haloperidol, olanzapine, paliperidone, risperidone, or placebo) were included in the main analyses. There was no evidence of sex differences in drug effects on overall symptoms (difference of standardised mean difference [DoSMD] 0·04, 95% CI -0·09 to 0·18). Dose-response curves were similar in females and males, plateauing at 3-5 mg risperidone equivalents, and the network meta-analysis showed no clear sex-specific treatment effects. Antipsychotics reduced all-cause dropout more in females than in males (ratio of odds ratios 0·74, 95% CI 0·56-0·98; moderate credibility). Prolactin increase was greater in females (DoSMD 0·83, 0·67-0·99; high credibility); other tolerability outcomes showed no clear sex difference.

INTERPRETATION: We found no evidence of sex differences in the efficacy or overall adverse event profiles, and no different dose-response relationships, for the drugs studied. However, we found some evidence that, among females, antipsychotics reduce all-cause dropout more, and increase antipsychotic-induced prolactin elevation versus placebo, as compared with males. Overall treatment efficacy estimates from previous meta-analyses are relevant to both sexes. To promote sex and gender equity, female participation in clinical trials and sex-stratified reporting should be encouraged.

title: Brain Stimulation Therapeutic Interventions in Neuropsychiatry: A Cambrian Explosion
abstract: Brain stimulation interventions alter neural activity by applying electrical, magnetic, sonic, or other forms of energy to the nervous system, using invasive or noninvasive methods. In recent years, the basic science and clinical science of neuromodulation have markedly advanced, and the evidence for clinical utility has resulted in new U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) clearance for multiple forms of brain stimulation and multiple indications in neuropsychiatry. This review summarizes the status of the major brain stimulation interventions for neuropsychiatric disorders, emphasizing key strengths and challenges in their therapeutic application. It also discusses opportunities for additional breakthroughs in treatment in this rapidly advancing field. These topics include noninvasive techniques for focal intracerebral drug delivery that bypass the adverse effects linked to systemic pharmacologic administration; interventions that noninvasively stimulate deep or superficial brain targets without impacting surrounding tissue; interventions that, in addition to or instead of altering symptomatic expression, reduce stress sensitivity, enhance resilience, and prevent manifestation of neuropsychiatric disorders; and the development of responsive or closed-loop stimulation techniques whereby the timing and nature of the stimulation are adjusted based on personalized biomarkers of future pathological brain states. Finally, noninvasive brain stimulation interventions intended for home use have recently shown clinical utility and have received FDA clearance. The field of brain stimulation represents a paradigm shift that is revolutionizing therapeutics and mechanistic understanding in neuropsychiatry.

title: Artificial Intelligence as the Computational Framework for Adaptive Closed-Loop Neuromodulation in Psychiatry
abstract: Adaptive neuromodulation offers a path toward personalized neuropsychiatric treatment by allowing therapy to respond to clinically meaningful neurophysiological and behavioral changes. Its clearest clinical precedents are responsive neurostimulation for epilepsy and adaptive deep brain stimulation for movement disorders. Both rely on signals that can be measured reliably and linked directly to stimulation. Psychiatric disorders pose a different problem: symptoms are heterogeneous, evolve over multiple timescales, and are observed only indirectly through noisy and incomplete measurements. Artificial intelligence can provide data-driven components of an adaptive neuromodulation system, connecting multimodal sensing, inference of patient state, prediction of treatment response, and constrained therapeutic adaptation. Interpretability is required throughout to support clinician and patient trust. Clinical evidence, however, remains limited to small proof-of-concept studies. Translation to practice will require replicated biomarkers and prospective multisite validation. It will also require explicit management of uncertainty and system designs that match adaptation to symptom and treatment timescales. Clinician and patient oversight must be preserved throughout, alongside safety constraints and governance across the treatment life cycle. This review presents a system-design view of how these components combine into a single adaptive architecture for psychiatric neuromodulation.

title: Endocannabinoid plasma concentrations and their relationship with clinical outcome and cannabis use in antipsychotic-naïve first episode psychosis
abstract: Disturbances in the endocannabinoid system (ECS) have been reported in psychosis, with evidence suggesting consistent alterations in N-arachidonoylethanolamine (anandamide; AEA) and inconclusive findings for 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG). Lower AEA concentrations have been associated with greater symptom severity, while the relationship between ECS and cannabis use remains unclear. However, the prognostic value of peripheral endocannabinoid concentrations for clinical outcomes and cannabis use in first-episode psychosis (FEP) remains largely unknown. This study examined whether baseline plasma endocannabinoid concentrations are associated with clinical outcomes and cannabis use at one-year follow-up in antipsychotic-naïve patients with FEP. Plasma AEA and 2-AG concentrations were measured in 58 antipsychotic-naïve patients. Psychopathology was assessed using the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS), and cannabis use was evaluated using Standard Joint Units to estimate THC consumption. Associations were examined using correlation and regression analyses adjusted for relevant covariates. Higher baseline AEA concentrations were associated with lower general psychopathology scores at follow-up. No significant associations were observed between endocannabinoid concentrations and total PANSS scores or positive and negative symptom subscales. Age emerged as a significant predictor of cannabis use at follow-up, while 2-AG showed a non-significant trend toward a higher likelihood of use. These findings suggest that higher baseline plasma AEA concentrations may be associated with a more favourable course of general psychopathology in early psychosis, potentially reflecting ECS involvement in stress- and anxiety-related symptom domains. Further studies are warranted to clarify the role of endocannabinoids in clinical outcomes and substance use trajectories in early phases of psychosis.

title: The burden of suicide by paraquat poisoning in Taiwan (1987-2017): trends, geographic variations, and demographic characteristics
abstract:
Background Pesticide self-poisoning accounts for 14%–20% of global suicides. Paraquat, a highly lethal pesticide, is involved in a considerable number of suicides in some countries. This study investigated the burden, trends, geographic variations, and demographic characteristics of pesticide and paraquat suicides in Taiwan. Methods Suicide data (1987, 1992, 1997, and 2002–2017) were obtained from Taiwan’s cause-of-death mortality data files. Trends and geographic variations in pesticide and paraquat suicides were examined using graphs and maps. Logistic regression was used to investigate the differences in the characteristics of pesticide versus non-pesticide suicides and paraquat versus non-paraquat pesticide suicides. Results Age-standardised pesticide suicide rates decreased by 74%, from 7.7 to 2.0 per 100,000, in 1987–2017. Paraquat was the leading agent involved in pesticide suicides, accounting for 59.9% (2,268/3,786) of pesticide suicides where the pesticide agents involved were recorded on the death certificate and at least 4.0% (2,268/56,361) of overall suicides in Taiwan. The percentage of paraquat suicides in overall suicides varied markedly across cities/counties (0.4%–15.6%). Pesticide suicides were more likely to be male, older people aged 65 + years, and from rural areas than non-pesticide suicides. By contrast, paraquat suicides tended to be younger than non-paraquat pesticide suicides, with no difference in sex distributions in the two groups. Conclusions The ban on paraquat implemented in 2018–2020 would have a significant impact on pesticide suicides and overall suicides, particularly in high-risk areas and demographic groups. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-026-29134-x .

Background Pesticide self-poisoning is a significant public health issue worldwide, accounting for 14%–20% of global suicides, or 110,000–168,000 deaths, annually [ 1 ]. Past research suggested marked variations in pesticide suicide rates over time [ 2 , 3 ], across different regions within a country [ 4 – 6 ], and across individuals of various demographic and socioeconomic characteristics [ 7 ]. Globally, the majority of pesticide suicides occur in the rural areas of countries in South East Asia and the Western Pacific region [ 1 , 8 ]. Pesticide self-poisoning is also among the most commonly used methods for suicide in Taiwan, with pesticides being the leading agents involved in poisoning-related suicides [ 9 ]. Pesticides commonly used in suicide vary markedly in case fatality [ 10 ]. Paraquat, a commonly used herbicide, is among the most lethal pesticides involved in self-poisonings [ 11 ], with a case-fatality ratio exceeding 70% in some studies [ 12 , 13 ]. Paraquat was found to be the most frequently ingested pesticide in South Korea and Taiwan, accounting for 35.5% and 34.7% of pesticide poisonings in previous hospital-based studies in South Korea (2008) and Taiwan (2012–2019), respectively [ 4 , 14 ]. However, few previous studies investigated the epidemiology of paraquat suicides based on population-based nationwide samples. Product-specific analyses of the characteristics of people who died by pesticide self-poisoning could inform prevention strategies targeted at regulating certain highly hazardous pesticides (HHPs), such as paraquat, and regulating or banning HHPs was recommended by the World Health Organization and Food and Agriculture Organization as among the most effective suicide prevention strategies [ 15 , 16 ]. In South Korea, for instance, the age-standardised rate of pesticide suicide fell annually by 28.2% between 2011 and 2014 following the ban on paraquat in 2011–2012 [ 2 ]. A systematic review of 27 studies from 16 countries showed that national bans on HHPs commonly used in self-poisonings appeared to be effective in reducing pesticide-specific and overall suicide rates, whilst the evidence for an effect of restricting HHPs sales to authorised users was less consistent [ 17 ]. In Taiwan, previous studies showed that suicide by pesticide poisoning decreased markedly (67%) between 1987 and 2010 [ 18 ], and pesticide suicide rates were greater in rural areas with a higher percentage of agricultural workers [ 19 ] and in males and older people [ 18 ] than their counterparts. The reduction in pesticide suicide rates in 1987–2010 was thought to be linked to the decrease in the agricultural population, but not to the bans of a number of pesticides during this period [ 18 ], as these pesticide bans did not include major pesticides found to be involved in pesticide suicides, such as paraquat [ 20 ]. Paraquat (24% soluble concentrate) was later banned in Taiwan in 2018–2020 in two stages—the import and production of paraquat were first banned in February 2018, and the sale and use of paraquat were completely banned in February 2020. However, there have been no previous national studies on the epidemiology of paraquat suicide, including its trends and geographic variations and the characteristics of people who died by paraquat self-poisoning, prior to the nationwide paraquat ban in Taiwan. Before implementing a pesticide ban aimed at reducing suicides, it is essential to identify the leading agent contributing to pesticide suicides and its burden. Additionally, the pre-ban burden of paraquat suicides across different sociodemographic groups and geographical areas is the basis for estimating the impact of a paraquat ban on suicide prevention. This study aimed to examine the burden of suicides by pesticide and paraquat poisoning before the paraquat ban (2018–2020) in Taiwan. Specifically, we investigated the contribution of paraquat self-poisoning to pesticide suicides in Taiwan, as well as the trends, geographic variations, and characteristics of people who died by pesticide self-poisoning, in particular paraquat self-poisoning, in 1987–2017. Methods Data We extracted suicide data for people aged 15 years or over from Taiwan’s cause-of-death data files, coded using the International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision (ICD-10), for years 1987, 1992, 1997, and 2002–2017. The ICD-10 includes a specific 3-digit code (i.e., ICD-10 X68) for suicide by pesticide poisoning. By contrast, in the International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Revision (ICD-9), suicides by pesticide poisoning were grouped with suicides using other solid or liquid substances under the 3-digit ICD-9 code E950. Taiwan officially started to use the ICD-10 in 2009, allowing the identification of pesticide suicides. To identify suicide by pesticide poisoning before 2009, we obtained ICD-10 coded cause-of-death data files for 1987, 1992, 1997, and 2002–2008 from the Ministry of Health and Welfare; these data were specially created for the preparation of the transition from the ICD-9 to the ICD-10; a previous study showed that the change in ICD revisions had little impact on the total number of suicide [ 21 ]. In this study, suicides were identified using the following ICD-10 codes: X60–X84 (suicide), Y10–Y34 (undetermined death), W75–W76 and W83–W84 (accident by suffocation), and X48 (accident by pesticide poisoning). A previous study from Taiwan showed that many of the deaths in the above alternative cause-of-death categories (i.e., undetermined death, accident by suffocation, and accident by pesticide poisoning) were likely to be misclassified suicides [ 22 ]. For the rest of the paper, the term ‘suicide’ referred to both certified suicides and possible suicides (undetermined deaths, accidental suffocation, or accidental pesticide poisoning) combined. Suicides by pesticide poisoning (‘pesticide suicides’) were identified using ICD-10 68 (suicide), Y18 (undetermined death), and X48 (accident); all other suicides were classified as ‘non-pesticide suicides’. The following variables were extracted from the cause-of-death data files: sex, age, date of death, and the city/county of registered residence. Age was grouped into four categories (15–24, 25–44, 45–64, and 65 + years). Individuals aged 15–24 years generally represent those who have recently entered the labour market, those aged 25–44 and 45–64 years correspond to individuals in the early and late stages of career development, respectively, and those aged 65 years and over are mostly retired. Based on the date of death, the season variable was created with the following categories–spring (March through May), summer (June through August), autumn (September through November), and winter (December through February). Geographic analyses were conducted at the city/county level, which corresponds to conventional administrative boundaries in Taiwan. More detailed geographic information was not available for pesticide suicide data. Taiwan’s 23 cities/counties were grouped according to the tertiles of the percentage of agricultural workers in the working population—as an indicator of rurality and ease of access to pesticides—resulting in three categories: urban (low percentage; 0.19%–1.16%), semi-rural (medium percentage; 1.21%–7.66%), and rural (high percentage; 9.31%–26.94%). Data for the percentage of agricultural workers were from the 2000 census. Among pesticide suicides, we extracted information on the pesticides involved from the original free text in the cause-of-death field on the death certificate. We grouped the pesticides according to the classification used by Taiwan’s Council of Agriculture, which used a matrix classifying each pesticide component based on the purpose of use (e.g., herbicide, insecticide, fungicide, rodenticide, etc.) and the chemical structure (e.g., organophosphate, carbamate, etc.) of the pesticides. An 11-category variable was created for the classification of pesticides commonly involved in suicides in Taiwan (Table S1 and Table S2); they included four groups of herbicides (paraquat, glyphosate, other herbicides, unspecified herbicides), four groups of insecticides (organophosphate, carbamate, other insecticides, unspecified insecticides), rodenticides, other pesticides, and ‘unspecified pesticides’ (i.e., the specific pesticides involved were not recorded on the death certificate although pesticide poisoning was certified as the cause of death). The ‘unspecified pesticides’ group was not included in the main analysis concerning the number and percentage of suicides involving different categories of pesticides. Detailed data for the cause-of-death free text on the death certificate were only available for the years 1987, 1992, 1997, and 2002–2012. By contrast, in 2013–2017, detailed data on the pesticide agents involved in suicide were not provided by the Ministry of Health and Welfare, although the number of paraquat pesticides and their percentage in all suicides could be calculated based on data provided by the Ministry of Health and Welfare, which compiled the data for the number of suicides by paraquat poisoning by year, sex, age (in 5-year bands), and city/county as part of its surveillance system to support suicide prevention strategies and monitor trends in paraquat suicide. Population data were extracted from the Demographic Fact Books (1987–2017) published by the Ministry of the Interior, Taiwan. Statistical analysis We calculated the age-standardised rates of pesticide suicide in each year using the World Health Organization (WHO) 2000 world standard population. The percentage of paraquat suicides (i.e., pesticide suicides by paraquat poisoning) in all pesticide suicides with known pesticide agents was calculated by year in 1987, 1992, 1997, 2002–2012, and its trend was examined graphically. The annual number and percentage of pesticide suicides using other categories of pesticides were also calculated. We calculated the number and percentage of pesticide suicides and paraquat suicides, overall and by sex, age group, and city/county with different levels of the percentage of agricultural workers in 2002–2017. Maps generated with ArcGIS Version 10.4 were used to examine the geographic variations in the rate and percentage (in all suicides) of pesticide suicides and paraquat suicides across the 23 cities/counties in Taiwan. We used Spearman’s correlation coefficients to investigate the correlation between the rates of pesticide and paraquat suicides and the percentage of agricultural workers in the working population across cities/counties. We used chi-square tests to compare the characteristics between pesticide and non-pesticide suicides, as well as between pesticide suicides involving paraquat (‘paraquat suicides’) and those involving other non-paraquat pesticides (‘non-paraquat pesticide suicides’). We did not include suicides by self-poisoning using unspecified pesticides ( n = 4927) and unspecified herbicides ( n = 192) in the categories of either paraquat suicides or non-paraquat pesticide suicides due to a lack of information on the specific pesticide agents involved to make such a distinction. Logistic regression analyses were used to investigate the association of demographic characteristics, season, and geographic area (grouped according to the percentage of agricultural workers) with pesticide suicide (versus non-pesticide suicide [reference group]) or paraquat suicide (versus non-paraquat pesticide suicide [reference group]). In subsequent multivariable analyses, we simultaneously adjusted for sex, age group, season, and geographic area to investigate whether these factors were independently associated with pesticide suicide or paraquat suicide. We conducted sensitivity analyses to examine the potential impact of suicide misclassification on the results by including data for certified suicides only (ICD-10 X60–X84) and excluding deaths of undetermined intent, accidental suffocation, or accidental pesticide poisoning. The comparison between paraquat and non-paraquat pesticide suicides was restricted to the years (1987, 1992, 1997, and 2002–2012) when detailed information about the pesticide involved in suicides was available; suicides using unspecified pesticides or unspecified herbicides were excluded from the analysis. A sensitivity analysis was conducted by excluding two cities/counties (i.e., Taichung City and Taichung County) from the comparison due to the high percentage of unspecified pesticide suicides (85.0% and 76.7%, respectively), indicating relatively low data quality in the two cities/counties. Because suicides using unspecified pesticides accounted for a substantial proportion (56.5%) of overall pesticide suicides, we conducted supplementary analyses to examine whether the city’s or county’s percentage of suicides using unspecified pesticides was associated with the proportion of paraquat suicides among specified pesticide suicides and the rate of paraquat suicides in the city/country, indicating differential certification practices in recording paraquat as the causative agent across cities/counties. title: The severity of dissociation and dissociative phenomena in non-affective psychosis: a systematic review and meta-analyses
abstract:
Background Non-affective psychosis is associated with elevated risk of suicide, self-harm, and reduced life expectancy. Symptoms of dissociation are common in non-affective psychosis, and dissociative experiences are known to be linked to multiple markers of elevated clinical risk, including sleep disturbance and negative affect. The present review represents the first comprehensive quantification of dissociative phenomena severity across multiple instruments in non-affective psychosis. Methods Six databases (Embase, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science) were searched from inception and systematically screened. Eligibility was established against ICD/DSM criteria or service-defined categorisation, including first-episode psychosis, brief limited intermittent psychotic symptoms, and at-risk of psychosis mental states. In total, data were extracted for 22 measures. Four random effects meta-analyses were conducted for measures with three or more independent datasets: the Dissociative Experiences Scale (DES) ( k = 51; n = 3,878); the Cambridge Depersonalization Scale (CDS) ( k = 6; n = 351); the Examination of Anomalous Self Experience scale, using the dichotomous scoring method (EASE-D) ( k = 11; n = 340); and the Examination of Anomalous Self Experience scale, using the continuous scoring method (EASE-C) ( k = 6; n = 235). Results DES data yielded a pooled mean of 21.28 (95% CI 19.19–23.38), consistent with moderately elevated dissociation. CDS data yielded a pooled mean of 36.38 (95% CI 26.89–45.87), also raised relative to community norms. EASE-D pooled means (M = 17.76 95% CI 15.29–20.24) and EASE-C pooled means ( M = 74.86 95% CI 52.36–97.35) both indicated high and clinically relevant loads of basic self-disturbance. High heterogeneity (I 2 > 85%) across measures highlights considerable variability in dissociative severity across samples, suggesting that levels of dissociation and dissociative experiences are not uniform in populations who experience non-affective psychosis. Conclusions The present findings emphasise the importance of assessing dissociation in non-affective psychosis, and where necessary, intervening clinically. Nonetheless, the development of trauma-informed, dissociation-targeted clinical interventions is required to optimise approaches to support. Throughout the literature, there is a pressing need for more harmonised measurement efforts and further mechanistic research. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s12888-026-08424-z .

Introduction Non-affective psychosis is an umbrella term which refers to a cluster of mental health conditions characterised by atypical perception, thought, and affect [ 1 ]. Contemporary diagnostic systems [ 2 , 3 ] describe non-affective psychosis in terms of positive symptoms , such as hallucinations, delusions, and disorganised thinking; negative symptoms , including apathy, anhedonia, and social withdrawal; and cognitive symptoms , such as inattention and memory difficulties. Unlike affective psychoses, non-affective psychoses are defined by the absence of a primary mood component [ 4 ]. Schizophrenia and related non-affective diagnoses, such as schizoaffective disorder and delusional disorder, are considered prototypical non-affective psychotic disorders, and the term schizophrenia spectrum disorder (SSD), covering all those conditions, is often employed interchangeably with non-affective psychosis [ 5 ]. In clinical settings, early intervention for psychosis services and community mental health teams support individuals diagnosed with SSD, and also those experiencing first episode psychosis (FEP), brief limited intermittent psychotic symptoms (BLIPS), or who present with ultra-high-risk (UHR) indicators for developing psychosis [ 6 ]. Notably, non-affective psychosis is associated with profound psychosocial and functional impairment [ 7 , 8 ], as well as markedly elevated risk of suicide, self-harm, reduced life expectancy, and excess premature mortality [ 9 – 11 ]. Against this background, there has been growing interest in the role of dissociative phenomena in the aetiology and phenomenology of non-affective psychosis, as well as their influence on outcomes [ 12 , 13 ]. As a concept, dissociation is difficult to define [ 14 ], however, it has been found to occur across multiple psychiatric disorders [ 15 ] and appears to be characterised by certain core components, including: derealisation , where a person feels the world is unreal; depersonalisation , where a person has feelings of being outside of themselves or somehow separated from their experiences; dissociative amnesia , characterised by gaps in memory; identity confusion , where a person finds it difficult to define themselves; and identity alteration , where a person switches noticeably between different aspects of their personality [ 16 – 19 ]. In non-affective psychosis specifically, recent work has conceptualised the core subjective experience of dissociation as a “felt sense of anomaly” (FSA) [ 20 , 21 ]. The investigating authors define this as “a subjective sense of strangeness” [ 21 ] which may take the form of unreality, disconnection, automaticity, or unfamiliarity, and occurs within one or more domains such as perception, identity, the body, and cognitions. Historically, SSDs and dissociative disorders have been framed as distinct diagnostic categories [ 13 ]. Nonetheless, systematic review evidence demonstrates substantial overlap, with symptoms of dissociation frequently present in SSDs, and the positive and negative symptoms typically associated with SSDs also commonly observed in dissociative disorders [ 13 ]. In parallel, dissociative experiences appear to be elevated in schizophrenia relative to healthy controls [ 17 ], and quantitative syntheses have provided evidence that dissociation is closely linked to the occurrence of psychotic symptoms. In one meta-analysis [ 22 ], a medium sized association between dissociative experiences and positive psychotic symptoms was reported ( r = 0.437), with significant symptom-specific relationships found for hallucinations ( r = 0.461), delusions ( r = 0.418), and paranoia ( r = 0.447). These findings extend earlier work focusing on auditory verbal hallucinations, which found a large, pooled correlation between voice hearing and dissociation across clinical and non-clinical samples ( r = 0.52) [ 18 ]. Together, this evidence supports that dissociative processes are not only common in people who experience psychosis but appear to be particularly and selectively related to positive symptoms. Converging evidence also links dissociation in psychosis to adverse childhood experiences. A meta-analysis of this relationship in severe mental illness [ 19 ] found a medium strength association between exposure to traumatic experiences in childhood and dissociation ( r = 0.33), with the association being strongest in SSD ( r = 0.39). All examined forms of adversity, including physical, sexual, and emotional abuse and neglect, were positively associated with dissociation, with emotional abuse emerging as a particularly robust correlate ( r = 0.41 in SSD). Recent psychosis-specific research replicated this finding [ 23 ], showing exactly the same level of medium association between developmental trauma and dissociation ( r = 0.33). This pattern is consistent with broader research exploring the link between trauma and psychosis [ 24 ], with recent evidence demonstrating a dose-response relationship between cumulative childhood adversity and psychosis risk [ 25 ]. These empirical findings have stimulated theoretical models in which dissociation is positioned as a key psychological process mediating developmental trauma and psychosis. A review of mediators between childhood adversity and psychosis identified post-traumatic sequelae, including dissociation and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms, as one of the main pathways through which adversity may increase psychosis risk and severity [ 26 ], as well as being candidate mechanisms underpinning the childhood trauma-psychosis association. Hence, understanding the role of dissociation in the development of psychosis may provide a potential opportunity to intervene early in the pathway to psychosis. Despite the expanding literature on dissociation in psychosis, important gaps remain. Existing reviews have largely focused on whether dissociation and psychotic symptoms correlate, or whether dissociation mediates associations between trauma and psychosis. To date, none have systematically quantified the severity of dissociative symptoms within non-affective psychosis, nor taken an approach which is inclusive of multiple measures of dissociation and dissociative phenomena. Given parallel calls to transform psychosis services through trauma-informed and mechanism-focused interventions [ 27 ], a clearer understanding of the severity of dissociation in non-affective psychosis is clinically pressing. Exploring how pronounced dissociation is in this group, and whether dissociative experiences vary across relevant characteristics, has implications for assessment, formulation, and the development of targeted interventions, as well as for ongoing debates regarding the boundary between psychotic and dissociative symptomatology. The aim of the present research, therefore, was to establish the severity of dissociation and dissociative phenomena in non-affective psychosis and explore potential influences on severity. Methods The current article reports one strand of a multi-faceted review on the nature, severity, and prevalence of dissociation in non-affective psychosis and relationships with suicide-related outcomes. A full prospective protocol for this wider review was published on the PROSPERO International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD420251010668) [ 28 ]. This review was conducted and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement [ 29 ]. Findings on suicide-related outcomes [ 30 ] and prevalence [ 31 ] are reported separately. Inclusion/exclusion criteria, search strategy, and extraction are presented for the wider systematic review [ 28 ]; however, this article reports on only the severity of dissociation and dissociative phenomena in non-affective psychosis. Because this review did not aim to evaluate intervention effects or scope a concept qualitatively, eligibility criteria is not optimally described using established eligibility frameworks such as PICO (population, intervention, comparator, outcome) [ 32 ] or PCC (population, concept, context) [ 33 ]. In line with guidance that review frameworks should be selected according to the review question rather than applied universally [ 34 ], it was decided on a bespoke framework for this multi-faceted review. Accordingly, inclusion/exclusion criteria are presented by population, phenomena, and evidence type. Inclusion criteria Population (I) Individuals described as having non-affective psychotic disorders, including ICD F20–F29 ‘schizophrenia and or other primary psychotic disorders’ [ 3 ], DSM-V ‘Schizophrenia Spectrum and Other Psychotic Disorders’ [ 2 ] or classified under relevant service-defined categories, including, first-episode psychosis, brief limited intermittent psychotic symptoms, and at-risk of psychosis mental states; and (II) Clinical participants, meaning persons would meet the criteria for or be receiving treatment from mental health services (e.g., outpatient clinics, inpatient settings, early intervention services, and community mental health teams). Phenomena (I) Studies exploring dissociative phenomena in non-affective psychosis, including depersonalisation, derealisation, amnesia, identity confusion, identity alteration, detachment, absorption, and felt sense of anomaly; (II) Studies providing severity estimates of dissociation assessed using validated measures, including, but not limited to: measures of broad dissociation, e.g., the Dissociative Experiences Scale (DES) [ 35 ], measures of specific dissociative experiences, e.g., the Cambridge Depersonalization Scale (CDS) [ 36 ], measures of anomalous self-experience, e.g., the Examination of Anomalous Self Experience scale (EASE) [ 37 ], psychosis population specific measures, including the Černis Felt Sense of Anomaly Scale (ČEFSA) [ 21 ], and dissociative disorder measures, including the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-V Dissociative Disorders, revised (SCID-D-R) [ 38 ]; (III) studies providing insight into the nature of dissociation in non-affective psychosis; (IV) studies which estimate the prevalence of dissociation in non-affective psychosis; and (V) studies which report on the role of dissociation in suicide-related outcomes in non-affective psychosis, including ideation, thoughts and behaviours, self-harm with suicidal intent, attempts, and completions. Evidence type (I) Quantitative studies, including observational studies, such as cross-sectional, cohort, and case-control studies, as well as experimental or interventionist studies that report dissociation-related measures in psychosis populations; (II) Qualitative studies that explore the experiences of dissociation in non-affective psychosis; and (III) Mixed-methods studies that combine qualitative and quantitative assessments of dissociation in non-affective psychosis. Exclusion criteria Population (I) Individuals described as experiencing affective psychoses (e.g., bipolar or mood disorders with psychotic experiences) or other co-morbid psychoses where non-affective psychosis or SSDs are not the primary diagnosis; and (II) Non-clinical or general population samples (e.g., student cohorts who were surveyed for psychotic-like experiences). Non-clinical samples were excluded to ensure diagnostic coherence and finding transferability, as self-reported psychotic-like experiences are known to differ in transience, severity, and quality from the psychotic experiences observed in diagnosable psychotic disorders [ 39 , 40 ]. Studies using healthy control comparators were included provided the clinical group met the review inclusion criteria. Where the sample was diagnostically mixed, these samples were included where ≥ 50% of participants aligned with non-affective psychosis diagnostic criteria. Phenomena (I) Studies which report on non-affective psychosis and/or suicide-related outcomes but do not contain a dissociation component; and (II) studies exploring non-suicidal self-harm [ 41 ]. title: Mental Health and Substance Use Disorder Expenditures in the US
abstract:
Key Points Question What were US mental health and substance use disorder expenditures in 2021-2023, and how were they distributed across disorders, populations, and services? Findings In this cross-sectional study of the 2021-2023 Medical Expenditure Panel Survey, annualized mental health care expenditures totaled $174 billion, representing 7% of all medical expenditures. Mood and anxiety disorders accounted for the largest aggregate expenditures, while expenditures per treated individual were highest for substance use disorders, schizophrenia, and bipolar disorder; ambulatory care accounted for most spending. Meaning Mental health expenditures vary widely across disorders, but they remain low relative to the societal burden of mental disorders.

Importance Understanding spending on mental health could help inform policymakers on decisions about where to direct mental health care resources and help evaluate whether spending aligns with public health priorities. Despite this, the magnitude and distribution of mental health expenditures in the US remain poorly characterized. Objective To estimate aggregate mental health expenditures by sociodemographic characteristics, type of insurance, mental health disorders, and type of service. Design, Setting, and Participants This was a cross-sectional analysis of the 2021-2023 Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS), an annual, nationally representative survey of the civilian noninstitutionalized US population. Analyses focused on individuals who made at least 1 outpatient mental health visit in 2021, 2022, or 2023. Data analysis was conducted from August 2025 to January 2026. Exposure Outpatient mental health visits. Main Outcomes and Measures Overall and per-100-person expenditures stratified by sociodemographic characteristics and diagnostic categories. Results The analysis included all survey participants (N = 67 532 person-year observations; mean [SD] age, 39.8 [0.25] years; 35 608 [50.7%] female) and identified those with reported outpatient mental health visits in 2021, 2022, and 2023 (n = 15 407; mean [SD] age, 45.0 [0.36] years; 9500 [60.0%] female). The estimated annualized aggregate total health care expenditures as measured in the MEPS in 2021-2023 were $2.5 trillion (95% CI, $2.3 trillion to $2.7 trillion), with $174 billion (95% CI, $152 billion to $196 billion) in mental health expenditures representing 7.0% (95% CI, 6.4%-7.7%) of all medical expenditures. This represented an annual mean of $523 (95% CI, $474-$571) per person overall and $2473 (95% CI, $2266-$2679) per person among those with any treated mental health disorder. Mood disorders and anxiety and fear-related disorders accounted for the highest aggregate expenditures ($74 billion [95% CI, $62 billion to $86 billion] and $69 billion [95% CI, $58 billion to $81 billion], respectively). Expenditures per treated individual were highest for substance use disorders ($9569 [95% CI, $6943-$12 195]), schizophrenia ($9370 [95% CI, $6685-$12 055]), and bipolar disorders ($7382 [95% CI, $6027-$8737]). Overall, expenditures on ambulatory services accounted for $107 billion (95% CI, $93 billion to $121 billion), while expenditures on medication accounted for $36 billion (95% CI, $31 billion to $40 billion) and those for home health care and inpatient treatment accounted for $20 billion (95% CI, $11 billion to $29 billion) and $12 billion (95% CI, $8 billion to $15 billion), respectively. Conclusions and Relevance This cross-sectional study found that expenditures on mental health disorders in the US vary widely at the per-person and population levels, but they are consistently low relative to the societal burden of mental disorders. Research that leads to more effective treatments, decreases provision of low-value care, and supports better matching of patients’ impairment with the appropriate level of care could help optimize treatment access while controlling expenditures.

This cross-sectional study evaluates US mental health and substance use disorder expenditures in 2021-2023 and how were they distributed across disorders, populations, and services.

title: National Trends in Benzodiazepine Dispensing
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Benzodiazepines (BZDs) are commonly prescribed medications in the United States. Up-to-date BZD dispensing trends can inform whether and where improvements in prescribing practices are needed. The objective of this study was to evaluate national changes in BZD dispensing from 2013 to 2024 by patient age and prescriber type.

METHODS: A repeated, cross-sectional analysis using the IQVIA Longitudinal Prescription dataset was conducted to examine trends in BZD prescription dispensing between 2013 and 2024 (a total of 1,100,233,787 prescription fills). BZD prescription fill counts, prevalence, and mean total dose dispensed per BZD prescription were reported annually, stratified by patient age and prescriber type.

RESULTS: From 2013 to 2024, the annual U.S. prevalence of BZDs dispensed declined by 26.7%, from 7.5% to 5.5%. Net decreases in prevalence occurred across age groups, with the largest relative reduction among young adults ages 18-29 (-44.8%). Primary care physicians dispensed the most BZD prescriptions, followed by advanced practice providers and psychiatrists/mental health specialists. There were sharp relative declines in the number of BZDs dispensed by pain medicine specialists (-62.5%), primary care physicians (-44.3%), and psychiatrists/mental health specialists (-38.3%), with an increase observed among advanced practice providers (+101.5%). The mean total dose dispensed per BZD prescription decreased across all patient ages and prescriber types, with large declines in doses prescribed by pain medicine specialists (-65.3%).

CONCLUSIONS: National declines in BZD prescription fills and total dose dispensed over the past decade may indicate greater caution or selectiveness in BZD dispensing, potentially related to safety considerations and drug labeling changes. Shifts in dispensing patterns among select patient and prescriber populations warrant ongoing monitoring.

title: Shared Transcriptional Features of Layer 3 Pyramidal Neurons Projecting to the Monkey Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Layer 3 (L3) pyramidal neurons projecting to the primate dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) convey essential information for core cognitive processes. Alterations in these neurons could contribute to cognitive deficits in schizophrenia. This study was designed to determine whether DLPFC-projecting L3 pyramidal neurons have a distinctive transcriptional profile.

METHODS: Laser microdissection was used to capture Nissl-stained and retrogradely labeled L3 pyramidal neurons that project to the DLPFC from the superior temporal cortex or posterior cingulate cortex of eight (four female) young adult (54-60 months of age) macaque monkeys. All samples were subjected to RNA sequencing. The results were compared to 1) data from L3 pyramidal neurons that project to the DLPFC from the posterior parietal cortex (lateral intraparietal cortex/area 7a [LIP/7a]) or contralateral DLPFC and 2) new single-nucleus RNA-sequencing data from multiple cortical regions of two female, young adult (77 and 96 months of age) monkeys and from similar publicly available human data.

RESULTS: Numerous genes (N=2,876) were differentially expressed between Nissl-stained L3 pyramidal neurons from the superior temporal cortex and posterior cingulate cortex. In contrast, only 527 genes were differentially expressed between DLPFC-projecting L3 pyramidal neurons from these regions. Transcriptional profiles were concordant between genes enriched in DLPFC-projecting L3 pyramidal neurons from the superior temporal cortex and posterior cingulate cortex and those enriched in DLPFC-projecting L3 pyramidal neurons from LIP/7a and contralateral DLPFC. The 91 genes enriched in samples from all four regions represent a transcriptional profile of DLPFC-projecting L3 pyramidal neurons. This profile was detected in specific clusters in both new monkey data and published human single-nucleus RNA-sequencing data from cortical regions that project to the DLPFC, but not from primary visual cortex (V1), which lacks these projections.

CONCLUSIONS: These findings indicate that DLPFC-projecting L3 pyramidal neurons can be identified by a shared transcriptional profile, regardless of cortical region. The transcriptional identification of these and other L3 pyramidal neurons with specific cortical projections will provide the means to determine which specific subtype or subtypes of pyramidal neurons contribute to cognitive impairments in schizophrenia.

title: Irritability in the Mix: An Exploratory Study of the Role of Irritability in Characterising Mood Disorders
abstract:
ABSTRACT Objectives To examine the relationship between irritability and mixed states in bipolar disorder to determine how subjective irritability and mixed symptoms of mania and depression manifest in patients with bipolar disorder over a period of 18 months. Methods This exploratory analysis examined longitudinal data from a randomised controlled trial of a psychological intervention for patients with bipolar disorder. Scores of subjective irritability and mood morbidity were analysed from data sampled over ten timepoints over the trial from 82 patients. Results Significant associations were found between the presence of irritability and mixed symptoms ( F (1, 684) = 20.468, p < 0.001). This relationship remained significant throughout the duration of the study and the administration of a psychological treatment which reduced both ratings of mood and irritability. Notably, when mixed symptoms are absent, irritability nevertheless remained for nearly half the time. Conclusions Irritability and mixed symptoms are phenomenologically linked. The persistence of this link, regardless of the existence of mixed symptoms, suggests that irritability permeates bipolar disorder and is core to its phenomenology. Future studies should interrogate the tethering of mixed symptoms and irritability in the context of bipolar disorder as this may lead to a deeper understanding of the core characteristics of the illness—both clinically and in terms of its neurobiology.

1 Introduction 1.1 Irritability as a Psychiatric Phenomenon Within psychiatry, irritability is a transdiagnostic phenomenon and a common clinical complaint among patients [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]. It is mentioned in over 30 different disorders within the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders—5th Edition Text Revision (DSM‐5‐TR) [ 4 ], serving as a feature and/or a diagnostic criterion. This ubiquity has led some to advocate for irritability disorders in adulthood to be considered a category of their own [ 5 ]. Indeed, irritability is so commonplace that its relationship to mental illnesses has been described as analogous to the relationship between fever and physical illnesses in general medicine [ 6 ]. This is because it is non‐specific, and its manifestation does not necessarily point to an underlying cause or mechanism. At the same time, its presence is often a strong signifier of illness and in practice it suggests that a person may require medical attention—hence it is an important indicator of illness. Although definitions of irritability vary, and there is no consensus [ 7 ], a recent working definition is that irritability is a mood characterised by a heightened sensitivity to stimuli coupled with a lowered threshold for responding with anger or aggression to typically less vexing stimuli [ 7 , 8 ]. It is often seen in the context of unmet needs (e.g., hunger, sleep), illness or somatic complaints (e.g., hormonal fluctuations) [ 9 , 10 ] and in phases of life in which the capacity to regulate one's emotions and moods is compromised (e.g., young childhood, dementia and Huntington's disease) [ 11 , 12 , 13 ]. Nevertheless, its nature within the context of psychiatric disorders remains largely unmapped. One hypothesis is that, rather than being a symptom of such a broad array of conditions with purportedly distinct aetiologies, it is an epiphenomenon that signals when there is a problem per se, but remains non‐specific to any underlying cause. In other words, irritability manifests when there is an underlying problem, but its manifestation is not specific to the underlying mechanisms that drive the problem, and irritability may instead be a secondary by‐product of this process. This possibility is worthy of further exploration, and just as fever is a useful clinical indicator, irritability too may serve as a broad signal for an underlying psychiatric condition. In this way, it may alert both patients and clinicians to an insidious problem before it crystallises and manifests acute symptoms. 1.2 Irritability in Mood Disorders Within our current major diagnostic taxonomies, the DSM‐5‐TR and the International Classification of Diseases 11th Revision (ICD‐11) symptoms of depression and mania have been separated and conceptualised as groups of symptoms from two diametrically opposed poles of mood [ 4 , 14 ]. However, irritability defies this separation in that it is listed within both sets of symptoms—as a symptom of mania in adults, and as a symptom of depression in children and adolescents. In addition, within DSM manic episode diagnostic criteria, if the prevailing mood during a manic episode is irritable (as opposed to euphoric), then there is a higher threshold required before a patient can be diagnosed with mania (four symptoms as opposed to the usual three) [ 4 ]. This distinct requirement and separation of irritability from other symptoms of mania perhaps indicates a tacit acknowledgment of irritability's lack of specificity. And whilst it is common enough in the context of bipolar disorder to be listed as a ‘symptom’ of mania, it is not specific enough to be counted as a mood that is ‘equal’ to euphoria. The higher threshold required of irritability is puzzling, as irritability is considered so central to manic symptomatology that it was listed as a key clinical feature (along with elevated mood and grandiosity, hyperactivity, pressured speech) in psychiatric textbooks published in the first half of the 20th century [ 15 ]. The prevalence of irritability among clinical presentations of mania has meant that its co‐occurrence with depressive symptoms is usually classified as a mixed presentation or episode. Indeed, in mixed depression, that is depressive episodes with so‐called ‘contra‐polar’ symptoms, irritability is considered one of the most prevalent (manifesting in approximately 30%–70% of presentations [ 16 , 17 ]) and is therefore classified as a key symptom of mixed states [ 16 , 17 , 18 ]. Thus, whilst irritability is in many ways non‐specific, it is at the same time characteristic of bipolar disorder presentations [ 19 ]. Therefore, the exact nature of irritability and its relationship to bipolar disorder as we currently understand it presents a quandary worthy of further exploration and characterisation. 1.3 The Status of ‘Mixity’ in Bipolar Disorder Whilst current diagnostic taxonomies remain largely wedded to the separation of manic and depressive symptoms, it is well‐established that clinically, many patients experience mixed symptoms (co‐occurring depressive and manic symptoms; also known as mixity [ 20 ]), with recent estimates ranging from 12%–28% of patients with a mood disorder experiencing mixed features [ 21 ]. The ability to classify mixed presentations as an ‘episode’ in and of themselves is a key point of distinction between DSM‐5‐TR and ICD‐11. In the latter, an episode of illness can be classified as a mixed episode if there are several ‘prominent’ symptoms from both depression and mania co‐occurring or alternating rapidly [ 14 ]. In DSM however, since the 5th edition in 2013, mood episodes can only be coded as depressed or manic, with contrapolar symptoms being coded as mixed ‘features’, thus minimising their importance [ 4 , 22 ]. Further, in DSM‐5, irritability cannot be counted as a manic/hypomanic symptom towards a mixed features specifier for a depressive episode. This inexplicable discrepancy between the centrality of irritability to mania and its absence within the mixed features criteria points towards a lack of clarity firstly, as regards the clinical characteristics of mixed states and secondly, the relationship between irritability and bipolar symptomatology. Therefore, our entire conceptualisation of bipolar disorder as being defined by mania, with or without depression, is challenged by the existence of mixed states [ 23 ]. The prevalence and the general lack of clinical and academic recognition of mixity in bipolar disorder has meant that mixed states are poorly understood [ 24 ]. This is reflected in outcomes for patients, with mixity being associated with poorer prognosis and response to treatments and an increased risk of impaired functionality and suicide [ 18 , 25 ]. Thus, advances in our understanding of mixity in bipolar disorder are urgently required to improve outcomes for patients through better detection, diagnosis and treatment. 1.4 Characterising Irritability and Bipolar Disorder In addition to mixed states comprising a significant proportion of bipolar presentations, in clinical practice, patients with bipolar disorder spend the majority of their time either in subsyndromal, euthymic phases of illness, or in periods between them, especially prior to the onset of the illness [ 26 , 27 ]. Thus, clear‐cut ‘pure’ forms of mania and depression form the minority of experiences for patients with bipolar disorder. Indeed, even within these pure forms, there are underlying factors of mixity; for example, 12%–29% of patients with pure mania show depressive symptoms [ 28 , 29 ]. Therefore, if we wish to improve our understanding of the illness it is imperative to identify the clinical symptoms that characterise the illness and can also be used for early detection, treatment and prevention. To this end, irritability provides a promising lead; it spans from normality through to the acute phases of illness and, at the same time, appears to be a key feature of mixity. Taken together, irritability may provide a potential avenue for early detection and management (see Figure 1 ). Another advantage of pursuing irritability as opposed to many other symptoms of bipolar disorder is that aside from being a common feature of the illness, it retains its appearance throughout the mood spectrum—manifesting as a consistent feature in different phases of the illness, as well as being present in subsyndromal periods (see Figure 2 ). In other words, symptoms can change in their appearance over the mood spectrum, such as psychomotor activity being excessive in mania or slowed in depression. Other symptoms manifest in one pole of the illness and may be absent in the other; for example, libido is increased during mania but diminished or absent altogether in depression. Irritability, on the other hand, is increased in both acute exacerbations of mood (mania and depression), and therefore can be measured in the same way across the phases of illness. In clinical practice, mixed states, which have been largely overlooked to date—are present for much of the time and it is here that irritability is likely to be found [ 18 ]. Therefore, in this study we examined a dataset to investigate our hypothesis that irritability is a core feature of bipolar disorder—because it is central to mixed states and spans subsyndromal presentations, which are the more consistent clinical state of the illness. 1.5 Aims In this preliminary analysis, we aimed to characterise the relationship between mixity and irritability in a population of patients with bipolar disorder. We hypothesise that irritability and mixity will be significantly correlated, suggesting a relationship between the manifestation of irritability in bipolar patients and the presence of mixed symptoms. 2 Methods This study utilised measures of irritability obtained from data from a psychological therapy trial which recruited adolescents and adults with bipolar disorder [ 30 ]. Detailed methodology is provided in the publication of this randomised controlled trial (RCT) of Interpersonal and Social Rhythm Therapy (IPSRT) versus a ‘control’ psychological intervention of Specialist Supportive Care (SSC) over 18 months [ 30 ]. Ethical consent for the original study and any subsequent analysis was obtained from the Canterbury Ethics Committee, and the trial was registered with the Australian and New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry (ACTRN12605000722695). Here, we summarise the key aspects pertinent to the current analysis. 2.1 Measures After obtaining consent, and prior to randomisation, the treating psychiatrist completed an Axis I diagnostic assessment using the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM‐IV (SCID) [ 31 ]. Throughout the 78‐week study, participants completed a series of questionnaires at 10 time points approximately every 9 weeks. Therefore, measurements were taken at weeks 0 (baseline), 8, 17, 26, 34, 43, 52, 61, 69 and 78. The questionnaires included a modified version of the self‐report Symptom‐Checklist 90 (SCL90), a 90‐item comprehensive psychological assessment of a broad range of psychopathology [ 32 ]. This assessment asks ‘During the past week, how much were you bothered by…’ for each item listed, which can be scored from 0 (not at all) to 4 (Extremely). Within the hostility subscale [ 33 ] there is an item that measures subjective irritability (item 11 – ‘Feeling easily annoyed or irritated’). This item was utilised as the irritability measure for the purposes of the current analysis. In order to chart the course of illness over the study period, participants completed the Longitudinal Interval Follow‐up Evaluation (LIFE) every 6 months. The LIFE was developed to retrospectively assess the longitudinal course of psychiatric disorders at regular intervals. The LIFE allows clinicians and researchers to assess the dates of individual episodes of a disorder and to rate the overall burden of symptoms. The validity of the LIFE in retrospectively determining mood state on a weekly basis has been demonstrated using the same cohort as the current analysis [ 34 ]. The LIFE asks participants to retrospectively rate their burden of mood symptoms on a weekly basis in an interview format, conducted at 6‐month intervals. Participants rated their mania and depression symptoms separately on a 0–5 scale where 0 = no symptoms, 1 = residual symptoms, 2 = partial remission, 4 = does not meet DSM criteria but has major symptoms or impairment and 5 = fulfils definite criteria for an ‘episode’ with the presence of either extreme impairment in functioning or psychotic symptoms. Ratings were carried out over the telephone by a trained research assistant who was blind to the treatment condition. For the current analysis, LIFE scores for depressive and manic symptoms for the 4 weeks immediately preceding and following each timepoint were calculated to correspond with the sampling of SCL‐90 scores. Figure 3 shows the timing of the collection for both the SCL and LIFE scores. A measure of ‘mixity’ was derived from the LIFE scores at each timepoint, wherein if a patient scored ≥ 0.5 for both depressive and manic symptoms at the same timepoint, mixity was determined to be present. A threshold of 0.5 was set as this would mean a patient would have had at least residual symptoms of both mania and depression for half of the sampling time for each timepoint (4 weeks pre and post).
