title: Holding collaboration together: a community response using a violence threat and suicide prevention protocol
abstract:
Coordinated, multi-sectoral community responses to youth mental health represent a promising yet undertheorized approach to addressing the service fragmentation that characterizes collaborative work across education, health, policing, and community services. This article presents qualitative findings from a larger sequential mixed-methods study of Strathcona County’s Violence, Trauma, and Suicide Prevention (VTSP) Protocol. The VTSP Protocol is a coordinated community framework designed to address youth mental health, community safety, and wellbeing in Alberta, Canada. The larger study combined social network analysis with qualitative inquiry; this article reports on the qualitative strand, which comprised 12 semi-structured interviews with key stakeholders purposively sampled from across the VTSP network. Thematic analysis of interview transcripts identified four interwoven themes that together describe the relational, communicative, and capacity-building labours through which the protocol is sustained: leadership as relational infrastructure, shared processes and communication structures, cross-sectoral relationships and joint purpose, and capacity building and shared language. Across all four themes, collaboration emerged not as a stable institutional achievement but as a fragile accomplishment, strong yet precarious, requiring continual renewal rather than resting on structural stability. The findings are theoretically grounded in Ecological Systems Theory and Relational Coordination Theory. Implications for the design, sustainability, and transferability of coordinated community response models in other communities and school authorities are discussed.

1 Introduction On February 10, 2026, five students and an educator were killed at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School in northeastern British Columbia in one of the deadliest school shootings in Canadian history, second only to the École Polytechnique massacre of 1989 ( 1 , 2 ). The perpetrator, an 18-year-old who had dropped out of school 4 years earlier, had a documented history of mental health concerns and had been the subject of multiple prior police contacts related to mental health ( 2 , 3 ). In the days following the tragedy, British Columbia Premier David Eby publicly stated that he would be seeking information from the provincial health system about what interactions it may have had with the perpetrator, a question that laid bare one of the most consequential failures in Canadian community safety: the absence of coordinated, sustained communication among the organizations responsible for identifying and supporting young people at risk ( 4 ). Tumbler Ridge is not an isolated case. The 2016 La Loche school shooting in Saskatchewan, in which a 17-year-old with known cognitive and social difficulties killed four people, raised the same fundamental question: what might have been different if schools, health services, police, and community organizations had been working together, sharing information through common protocols, and taking coordinated action before a crisis became a catastrophe ( 1 ). These events, rare by international standards but devastating in their impact, are powerful reminders that the systems responsible for youth mental health, community safety, and violence prevention are often fragmented precisely when integration is most urgently needed. The urgency that these tragedies reveal is inseparable from a broader pattern of deteriorating youth mental health across Canada. Data from the 2023 Canadian Health Survey on Children and Youth indicate that the proportion of young people aged 16 to 21 rating their mental health as fair or poor more than doubled between 2019 and 2023, rising from 12 to 26% ( 5 ). Longitudinal surveillance data document sustained increases in diagnosed mood and anxiety disorders, suicidality, and mental health service utilization among youth aged 12 to 24 between 2011 and 2018 ( 6 ), and Canadian Institute for Health Information ( 7 ) data indicate that mental health disorders account for approximately 5% of all emergency department visits among children and youth aged 5 to 24. The burden is not evenly distributed. According to the 2022 Mental Health and Access to Care Survey, 56% of 2SLGBTQ + youth met diagnostic criteria for a mental health or substance use disorder, and Indigenous youth experience depression and suicide at rates 5 to 7 times higher than those of non-Indigenous peers ( 8 ). For these young people, early identification and coordinated support are not merely beneficial; they are potentially lifesaving. Despite the scale and urgency of this challenge, the systems responsible for addressing youth mental health remain deeply fragmented. Schools, health services, policing, and community organizations each carry distinct mandates, operate under separate legislation and governance structures, and frequently use incompatible professional languages and referral pathways. Surveys of educators consistently identify the lack of coordination between schools and community mental health services as a primary barrier to effective student support ( 9 , 10 ). Research from Sweden, examining cross-boundary collaboration in youth mental health systems, concluded that there is little scientific evidence on how these collaborations are applied or sustained, and that significant gaps persist between the needs of young people and the quality and accessibility of available services ( 11 ). In the Canadian context, these gaps are compounded by workforce shortages, uneven regional resourcing, and the absence of a national framework for coordinating cross-sector responses to youth mental health ( 10 ). The result is a system in which information about a young person in crisis rarely travels across the organizational boundaries that divide education from health, health from policing, and policing from community services. The consequences of that fragmentation are not abstract. What makes coordinated, multi-sector community responses both compelling and rare is precisely the organizational complexity they must overcome. Bringing together education, health, policing, and community services around a shared protocol, common language, and sustained relational infrastructure requires deliberate design, ongoing resourcing, and the cultivation of trust across boundaries that ordinarily separate these sectors. In practice, most communities do not have such systems in place. Where they do exist, they typically involve a small number of organizations operating under limited agreements. The Strathcona County Violence, Trauma, and Suicide Prevention (VTSP) Protocol is an exceptional case: a coordinated community framework in which 16 organizations from across education, health, policing, and community services have worked together, using the Violence Threat Risk Assessment (VTRA) and Threat Evaluation of Situations (TES) processes as shared methodology and language, to address youth mental health, community safety, and wellbeing. Operationally, the protocol is sustained through regular cross-agency meetings, shared processes and forms, designated community leads, and ongoing VTRA and TES training; when coordinated action is required, community leads help gather information, bring relevant partners together, and guide the collaborative process. The protocol was built, in part, in direct response to a traumatic community event, and it has received national recognition as a promising model for other communities and school authorities in Alberta and across Canada. Its existence represents an organizational and relational achievement that the vast majority of Canadian communities have not yet attained. This article reports qualitative findings from a larger sequential mixed-methods study of the VTSP Protocol. The larger study combined social network analysis of 25 respondents across 16 core organizations with the qualitative inquiry reported here. The qualitative strand comprised 12 semi-structured interviews with key stakeholders drawn from across education, policing, and community services within the VTSP network. While a growing body of scholarship addresses multi-sector collaboration and collective impact in social and health systems ( 12–14 ), three important gaps remain in the literature. First, existing research attends predominantly to the structural conditions that enable collaboration to begin, rather than to the relational, communicative, and capacity-building labour through which it is maintained and renewed over time. How collaboration is sustained across multiple sectors, particularly in communities that must navigate staff turnover, jurisdictional ambiguity, information-sharing legislation, and periodic crises, remains comparatively undertheorized. Second, qualitative research that examines the lived experience of practitioners working within coordinated community protocols that span education, health, policing, and community services is scarce. Most collaborative governance research operates at the level of policy analysis or program evaluation; the practitioner perspectives that illuminate how shared processes, trust, leadership, and language function in daily practice are underrepresented. Third, in-depth, community-specific qualitative research on coordinated community responses to youth mental health in the Canadian context is limited, particularly in jurisdictions governed by Alberta’s Protection and Privacy Act and Access to Information and Privacy, where legislative conditions create distinct dynamics for cross-sector information sharing that may differ meaningfully from those studied in the United States and Europe. This article addresses these gaps by offering a theoretically grounded, qualitative account of how collaboration is sustained within a coordinated community response to youth mental health and community safety. Drawing on thematic analysis of 12 in-depth interviews, the study identifies four interwoven themes: leadership as relational infrastructure, shared processes and communication structures, cross-sectoral relationships and joint purpose, and capacity building and shared language. A central interpretive finding is that collaboration within the VTSP Protocol is not a stable institutional achievement but a fragile accomplishment, strong yet precarious, requiring continual renewal rather than resting on structural stability alone. In a national context where the consequences of fragmented community responses can be measured in lives, this finding carries direct implications for how coordinated community responses to youth mental health are designed, resourced, and sustained over time. 1.1 Guiding questions and system-level relevance The research questions that guided this study were developed in response to the evidence that coordinated community responses to youth mental health, though demonstrably valuable, are rarely examined in depth from the perspective of those who sustain them. Understanding how collaboration is practiced and maintained within such a protocol, and what strategic and relational conditions underpin its success, has direct implications for communities seeking to build or strengthen similar models. This article is oriented by two research questions: How do the key stakeholders and organizations within Strathcona County’s VTSP Protocol collaborate and exchange information to address the mental health and wellbeing of children and youth? What are the underlying strategies and relational dynamics that contribute to the success of Strathcona County’s VTSP Protocol as a coordinated community response, and how can these insights inform the development of similar models for other communities and school authorities in Alberta? These questions are grounded in a recognition that the VTSP Protocol operates as a system-level response to challenges that no single organization can address alone. Youth mental health, violence prevention, and community safety sit at the intersection of education, health, policing, and community services, and effective responses require that these sectors share information, align their actions, and sustain coordination across the organizational boundaries that ordinarily separate them. The first research question attends to the structural and relational dimensions of that coordination, examining how collaboration and information exchange are enacted in practice across 16 organizations with distinct mandates and professional cultures. The second question moves from description to explanation and implication, probing the deeper strategies and relational conditions that enable the protocol to function as a coherent, sustained response rather than an episodic or fragmented one, and asking what lessons can be drawn for the many Alberta communities and school authorities that have not yet developed such capacity. The system-level relevance of this inquiry extends beyond Strathcona County. At a time when the deterioration of youth mental health is well documented nationally ( 6 , 15 ), and when high-profile tragedies have repeatedly exposed the costs of fragmented community responses, the question of how to build, sustain, and transfer integrated multi-sector frameworks has acquired considerable urgency. This study contributes to that question by providing a theoretically grounded, qualitative account of the relational, communicative, and capacity-building labours that hold such a framework together, offering both conceptual insight and practical implications for communities, school authorities, and policymakers seeking to strengthen cross-sector coordination in support of children and youth. 2 Theoretical framework This study is grounded in two complementary theories serving distinct purposes: Bronfenbrenner’s Ecological Systems Theory and Relational Coordination Theory. Together, these theories provide a foundation for understanding both why a coordinated community response is necessary and how such a response is sustained in practice. Ecological Systems Theory provides a contextual frame for understanding youth mental health, trauma, violence prevention, and suicide prevention as concerns shaped across multiple interacting environments, while Relational Coordination Theory provides an interpretive lens for examining how organizations working across boundaries coordinate their actions through relationships and communication. 2.1 Ecological systems theory Bronfenbrenner’s Ecological Systems Theory conceptualizes child and youth development as embedded within nested and interacting systems, including the microsystem, mesosystem, exosystem, macrosystem, and chronosystem ( 16 , 17 ). title: Transferable Design Principles for Scalable Mental Health Systems: A Conceptual Framework Informed by Innovations Across African Contexts
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Mental disorders are a leading cause of disability worldwide, and their burden continues to increase across Africa. Despite growing need, access to care remains limited, with treatment gaps reaching up to 90% in some settings. These gaps reflect longstanding constraints in workforce, financing, infrastructure, and sociocultural factors, alongside uneven policy implementation. At the same time, countries and communities across the continent are developing new approaches to mental health care that can complement conventional, specialist-centered models and offer transferable lessons for mental health system transformation globally.

OBSERVATIONS: This Special Communication proposes 4 transferable design principles for scalable and culturally responsive mental health systems, synthesized into a comprehensive conceptual framework and context-sensitive implementation road map: (1) workforce and educational transformation, (2) community-based care architecture, (3) systems integration, and (4) cultural and pluralistic care. Evidence from multiple African countries demonstrates that nonspecialist clinicians, including community health workers and peer supporters, can deliver screening and brief psychological interventions when reinforced by training and supervision. Community-based models are increasingly shifting care closer to where people live, incorporating recovery-oriented approaches that emphasize social reintegration. Integration of mental health into primary care, HIV services, and maternal health platforms has shown promise, though sustainability remains dependent on broader health system capacity. At the same time, pluralistic care systems, in which individuals engage biomedical and traditional professionals, highlight the need for approaches that are culturally responsive and grounded in human rights. Across these design principles, progress is evident, but implementation remains uneven, and much of the current evidence is limited by short-term evaluations and reliance on symptom-based measures.

CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Closing the treatment gap in Africa will require more than scaling existing services. It will depend on strengthening locally led research and context-sensitive implementation, embedding innovations within national systems, and investing in workforce development, supervision, and governance. African mental health innovations are not only responses to constrained resources, but also contributions to the broader understanding of how scalable, equitable, and culturally responsive mental health systems can be designed across diverse global settings.

title: Proteomic Signatures in Major Depressive Disorder and Depression Symptom Subtypes
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is biologically heterogeneous and encompasses diverse symptom presentations. The authors used large-scale plasma proteomics to examine proteomic associations with categorical MDD status, continuous depression symptom severity, and DSM-IV-defined melancholic and atypical symptom dimensions.

METHODS: Using the SomaScan platform, the authors conducted plasma proteomic profiling of 7,289 analytes in 1,881 participants from the Netherlands Study of Depression and Anxiety, including individuals with current MDD (N=469), individuals with remitted MDD (N=918), and healthy control subjects (N=494). They evaluated associations with diagnostic status, symptom severity, and melancholic and atypical symptom dimensions, followed by pathway enrichment analyses.

RESULTS: Eight aptamers, representing seven unique proteins, differed significantly between the current MDD and healthy control groups after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Overall depression symptom severity was associated with 18 significant aptamers corresponding to 18 unique proteins, whereas atypical symptoms were associated with 58 significant aptamers corresponding to 57 unique proteins. In contrast, no individual proteins reached FDR significance for melancholic symptoms. Pathway analyses showed enrichment for extracellular matrix organization, collagen formation, complement cascade signaling, platelet activation, and hemostasis in relation to overall depression symptom severity. Gene set enrichment analysis of proteins ranked by association with melancholic symptoms identified pathway-level enrichment despite the absence of FDR-significant individual proteins, including mitochondrial stress response, protein translation, complement signaling, and nervous system development. Atypical symptoms showed enrichment of extracellular matrix organization, collagen formation, complement cascade signaling, insulin-like growth factor transport, and chromatin regulatory processes.

CONCLUSIONS: These findings support biological heterogeneity within MDD and suggest that peripheral proteomic alterations are more strongly represented for specific symptom dimensions than for categorical diagnosis alone. Atypical symptoms showed pathway-level enrichment with significant individual protein associations. A dimensional framework may improve biological stratification of depression and refine biomarker-informed approaches to clinical symptom profiles.

title: Connectomic Determinants of Subcallosal Cingulate Deep Brain Stimulation for Depression
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Subcallosal cingulate (SCC) deep brain stimulation (DBS) has shown promise for treatment-resistant depression. This study retrospectively evaluated a large curated SCC-DBS dataset to identify connectomic factors associated with sustained clinical improvement across patients, focusing on the white matter bundles consistently implicated in patient-specific connectome-based targeting.

METHODS: A total of 131 patients (mean age=46.67 years, SD=9.79; 60.31% female) with treatment-resistant depression from three independent cohorts received bilateral SCC-DBS using site-specific targeting methods. Clinical improvements were assessed using the 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAM-D). Based on individual DBS settings, volumes of tissue activated were reconstructed, and voxel-wise stimulation mapping and normative fiber-wise analyses were performed to assess contributions of white matter bundles to therapeutic response.

RESULTS: Responders (patients with ≥50% reduction in HAM-D score) exhibited a less variable spatial distribution of volumes of tissue activated than nonresponders. Probabilistic stimulation mapping identified a focal cluster associated with clinical improvement. Fiber-wise analyses showed that stimulation of predefined white matter tracts targeted by connectome-based SCC-DBS contributed to clinical efficacy. Notably, failure to activate the left cingulum bundle and medial uncinate fasciculus decreased the therapeutic effects of SCC-DBS.

CONCLUSIONS: This study highlights the significance of stimulating critical white matter bundles for effective SCC-DBS. Available evidence supports the idea that precisely targeting the lateralized cingulum bundle and medial uncinate fasciculus is essential for sustained clinical improvement. These findings suggest potential advantages of connectome-based targeting for SCC-DBS over targeting based solely on anatomical landmarks or normative atlases, using a method that is precise, reliable, and scalable for future use in individual patients.

title: National prevalence and sociodemographic correlates of potential depression, anxiety, and suicidality among the young population in Kazakhstan: a national population-based study
abstract:
Background Mental health disorders are the primary driver of the global disease burden among young people, yet nationally representative data for Central Asia remains scarce. This study aimed to determine the prevalence and sociodemographic correlates of potential depression, anxiety, and suicidality among the young population in the Central Asian nation of Kazakhstan. Methods A cross-sectional analysis was conducted using data from the 2024 Kazakhstan Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS), a nationally representative, multi-stage probability sample. Potential depression and anxiety were screened using the PHQ-2 and GAD-2 instruments (cut-off ≥ 3), while suicidality was assessed via self-reported thoughts (past two weeks) or attempts (past 12 months). Weighted prevalence estimates were calculated, and modified Poisson regression models identified independent sociodemographic risk factors. Population attributable fractions (PAFs) were estimated to quantify the impact of associated risks. Findings We included 5,079 individuals aged 15–24 years. The weighted national prevalence was 1.70% (95%CI = 1.31–2.08) for potential depression, 1.59% (95%CI = 1.23–1.96) for potential anxiety, and 0.96% (95%CI = 0.65–1.27) for potential suicidality among the population aged 15–24 years. In adjusted analyses, female sex was the strongest predictor of both potential depression (adjusted risk ratio [aRR] = 2.72, 95%CI = 1.55–4.79) and anxiety (aRR = 2.80, 95%CI = 1.58–4.96). Non-Kazakh ethnicity was also significantly associated with an increased risk of depression (aRR = 1.88, 95%CI = 1.17–3.02) and anxiety (aRR = 1.99, 95%CI = 1.28–3.11). PAFs indicated that female sex accounted for 45.6% and 46.8% of the risk for depression and anxiety, respectively. No significant sociodemographic correlates were identified for suicidality. Conclusion These findings provide the first nationally representative benchmarks for youth mental health in Kazakhstan. While prevalence rates are lower than global averages, the marked disparities by sex and ethnicity highlight the need for targeted, culturally sensitive mental health interventions. Strengthening early detection and resource allocation for these vulnerable subgroups is essential to meet national and Sustainable Development Goal targets. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-05618-8 .

Introduction Adolescent mental health represents a global public health priority, as psychiatric disorders during this developmental window are primary drivers of morbidity and mortality, notably through suicidality [ 1 ]. Anxiety and depressive disorders frequently emerge during adolescence and young adulthood, often following a chronic or relapsing course if left unaddressed. Globally, approximately 300 million individuals aged 5–24 years live with a mental health disorder, contributing nearly 30 million years lived with disability (YLDs) [ 2 ]. Furthermore, suicide remains a leading cause of death among those aged 15–29 years, with 75% of these fatalities occurring in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) [ 3 ]. In Eastern Europe and Central Asia, suicide is the foremost cause of mortality in the young population [ 4 ]. Despite the significant disease burden, a recent scoping review highlighted that mental health research is critically under-prioritized within public health systems across Central Asia [ 5 ]. To date, empirical data regarding mental health difficulties among youth aged 15–24 years in this region remain sparse [ 6 ]. Evidence suggests that youth suicide is an escalating crisis in Kazakhstan [ 7 ]; according to the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), the risk of suicidal behavior among Kazakhstani adolescents (15–19 years) is three times higher than the average across the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), a regional organization in Eurasia [ 8 ]. While the prevalence and sociodemographic correlates of depression and anxiety have been extensively documented in other global contexts [ 9 ], [ 10 ], these parameters remain insufficiently characterized in Kazakhstan. Existing literature has predominantly focused on adult cohorts or specific administrative regions [ 11 – 13 ]. For instance, a cross-sectional survey of 1,021 adults during the COVID-19 pandemic identified a 12.0% prevalence of depression and 8.4% for anxiety [ 14 ]. Another study in the Karaganda Region reported depressive symptoms in 75.7% of adults, with higher rates observed in females [ 13 ]. Untreated mental disorders are associated with profound adverse outcomes, including educational attrition, diminished economic productivity, and increased risk of incarceration or homelessness, impacting both the individual and broader society [ 15 ], [ 16 ]. Current evidence in Kazakhstan is largely derived from small-scale regional surveys, leaving a critical gap in nationally representative epidemiological data. The 2024 Kazakhstan Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) marked a significant milestone by including a dedicated mental health module for participants aged 15–24 years. Such data are fundamental for informing evidence-based prevention strategies and achieving Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) Target 3.4, which mandates the promotion of mental health and well-being across the lifespan [ 17 ]. This study aims to investigate the prevalence and sociodemographic correlates of potential depression, anxiety, and suicidality among young people aged 15–24 years in Kazakhstan using a nationally representative sample. We specifically address two research questions: (1) What is the national prevalence of these conditions among Kazakhstani youth? and (2) Which sociodemographic factors—including age, sex, residence, education, marital status, and household wealth—independently associate with these outcomes? Method Study design and participants This study utilized a cross-sectional, population-based design analyzing data from the 2024 Kazakhstan Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS), which was implemented by the Bureau of National Statistics of Kazakhstan with technical and financial support from UNICEF to collect critical health and development indicators. To ensure the robust tracking of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and national health development, the survey employed a two-stage, stratified cluster sampling design, generating representative estimates at the national, regional, and urban-rural levels across all 17 regions and three major municipalities of Kazakhstan. In the first stage, census enumeration areas were systematically selected within urban and rural strata with probability proportional to size. In the second stage, households were systematically selected within each enumeration area. Eligible household members were interviewed using standardized questionnaires, including a household questionnaire administered at the household level and individual questionnaires administered to specific population groups (women aged 15–49 years, men aged 15–24 years, children aged < 5 years, and children aged 5–17 years). All questionnaires were administered by trained data collectors following the MICS7 protocol to ensure international comparability. Overall, 22,454 households were successfully interviewed (response rate 96.3%), with response rates of 97.4% for women and 94.4% for men aged 15–24 years. For this study, we used data from the men’s and women’s questionnaires, restricted to individuals aged 15–24 years. Participants were excluded from the analysis if more than 50% of items were missing on either the brief depression or anxiety scales, resulting in a final analytical sample of 5,079 participants (Supplementary Fig. 1 ). Verbal informed consent was obtained from all participants. For respondents aged 15–17 years, parental or guardian consent was obtained prior to the participant’s assent. A detailed description of the survey methodology can be found in the Kazakhstan MICS 2024 report, available on the UNICEF MICS website [ 18 ]. Outcome measures Potential depression and anxiety were evaluated using two validated brief screening instruments: the 2-item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-2) and the 2-item Generalized Anxiety Disorder Scale (GAD-2), both of which are recognized as being as effective as their longer versions for rapid initial screening [ 19 ], [ 20 ]. While formal validation of these instruments in Kazakhstan is limited, evidence from systematic reviews and meta-analyses supports the reliability and validity of ultra-brief screening instruments across diverse cultural and international settings [ 20 ], [ 21 ]. The PHQ-2 assessed the frequency of depressed mood—defined by feelings of sadness and hopelessness—and anhedonia—defined as the loss of pleasure or interest in previously enjoyable activities—over the preceding two weeks. The GAD-2 evaluated feelings of being nervous, anxious, or on edge, alongside the inability to stop or control worrying. All items were rated on a four-point Likert scale ranging from 0 (not at all) to 3 (almost every day), with total scores for each scale ranging from 0 to 6; a cut-off point of ≥ 3 was used to indicate potential depression or anxiety [ 22 ]. More details about the depression and anxiety measures available in Supplementary Table 1 . Suicidality was assessed as a binary variable based on participants’ self-reported thoughts and behaviors. Participants were classified as having suicidality if they responded affirmatively to having tried to harm themselves with the intention to end their life in the past 12 months, or having thought about doing something to end their life in the past two weeks. Sociodemographic variables In this study, we considered the following sociodemographic factors based on prior literature [ 23 ]. The primary independent variables included age (stratified as 15–19 and 20–24 years), sex (male or female), and area of residence (urban area or rural area). Educational attainment was categorized into high school and below or college and above, while marital status was divided into married or unmarried. Household wealth quintiles were developed by MICS for each survey using a wealth index based on principal component analysis (PCA) of household characteristics, including dwelling conditions, access to water and sanitation, and ownership of consumer goods. To ensure adequate sample sizes within each category and improve the statistical stability of the estimates, our study further classified into low, middle, and high tiers. Ethnicity was recorded as either Kazakh or non-Kazakh ethnicities. More details about these variables available in Supplementary Table 1 . Statistical analysis The proportion of missing data for the included variables was minimal, remaining below 1% for potential depression (0.2%), anxiety (0.1%), and suicidality (0.2%). These missing values were addressed using multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE) with five imputations performed via the ‘mice’ package in R, incorporating all independent and outcome variables to minimize bias. Descriptive statistics were used for all outcomes, with continuous data reported as mean values and standard deviations, while categorical data were presented as frequencies and percentages. Associations between categorical variables were tested using Pearson’s chi-square test with Rao & Scott adjustment to account for the complex survey design. All analyses incorporated weighting and clustering by enumeration district using the R survey package to ensure national representativeness [ 24 ]. To identify independent risk factors, modified Poisson regression models were applied for each outcome, with results reported as adjusted risk ratios (aRRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) [ 25 ]. This approach was chosen to directly estimate risk ratios, which provide more interpretable measures of association and are consistent with the estimation of population attributable fractions (PAFs). Weighted prevalence estimates were visually presented in plots displaying age-sex and area-sex stratified patterns and highlighting group-specific differences, with 95% CI. Prevalence by region was illustrated on maps to visualize spatial patterns of the outcome. Sensitivity analyses were conducted on unimputed data to confirm the robustness of the primary findings. All statistical procedures were performed using R version 4.3.2 with a significance threshold of p < 0.05. Results Prevalence of potential depression, anxiety, and suicidality A total of 5,079 young individuals aged 15–24 years were included in the final analytical sample. Compared with excluded participants, included participants differed significantly in marital status ( p < 0.001) and residence ( p = 0.012), and no significant differences were observed in age, sex, education, wealth, and ethnicity (Supplementary Table 2 ). Population estimates (weighted percentages) indicated that the study population was predominantly 15–19 years (58.0%), resided in urban areas (67.6%), was comprised of unmarried individuals (85.6%), and was of Kazakh ethnicity (72.4%) (Table 1 ). Overall, the weighted national prevalence was 1.70% (95% CI 1.31–2.08) for potential depression, 1.59% (95% CI 1.23–1.96) for potential anxiety, and 0.96% (95% CI 0.65–1.27) for potential suicidality. In bivariate analyses, potential depression and anxiety were significantly more frequent among individuals aged 20–24 years ( p = 0.012), females ( p < 0.001), unmarried participants (depression: p = 0.004; anxiety: p = 0.009), and those of non-Kazakh ethnicity (depression: p = 0.005; anxiety: p = 0.002). Conversely, no significant sociodemographic differences were observed for the prevalence of potential suicidality. Sex and age-specific variations Stratified analyses revealed that sex-specific differences in the prevalence of potential depression and anxiety were maintained across age groups (Fig. 1 ). Among participants aged 15–19 years, females reported a significantly higher prevalence of potential depression (1.8% vs. 0.8% in males; p = 0.038) and potential anxiety (1.9% vs. 0.6% in males; p = 0.007). title: Two-year domain-specific cognitive trajectories following a first episode of psychosis and early intervention: A data-driven study
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND HYPOTHESIS: Cognitive impairment is a core feature of psychotic disorders and predicts long-term outcomes. However, cognitive trajectories following first-episode psychosis (FEP) are heterogeneous. We hypothesized the presence of distinct global and domain-specific cognitive trajectories over two years, with differential baseline predictors and distal outcomes associated with trajectory membership.

STUDY DESIGN: Data were drawn from the RAISE-ETP study (N = 404, aged 15-40). Cognition was assessed with the Brief Assessment of Cognition in Schizophrenia (BACS) at baseline, 12, and 24 months. Latent growth modelling was used to identify trajectory classes for global cognition and six individual cognitive domains.

STUDY RESULTS: Cognitive trajectories were largely stable, with modest improvements. Two trajectories emerged for global cognition, verbal fluency, motor speed and working memory; three for executive function and processing speed; four for verbal memory. Higher education was associated with less impaired classes across global cognition (OR = 0.34, 95% CI 0.20-0.59) and all domains. Less impaired cognitive trajectories were linked to higher quality of life (SMD = -0.91, 95% CI -1.42--0.39) and lower symptom severity. Associations with depressive symptoms were heterogeneous: greater severity accompanied more impaired working memory and executive function trajectories but less impaired motor speed, verbal memory, and verbal fluency trajectories.

CONCLUSIONS: Class membership was primarily differentiated by baseline cognitive performance; baseline individual differences may contribute to heterogeneity in clinical and functional outcomes. Domain-specific analyses revealed associations with clinical outcomes not apparent from global cognition alone, highlighting the importance of early identification and personalized cognitive interventions in FEP.

title: Network adaptability governs resilience and susceptibility to social defeat
abstract: Stress resilience-the ability to maintain mental health after adversity-manifests in humans and rodents as efficient threat-safety discrimination and fear extinction. Although behavioral differences between resilient and susceptible individuals are well documented, the brain-wide structural signatures that distinguish resilience, susceptibility, and impaired threat learning remain poorly defined. Using a translational mouse model of chronic social defeat stress in male C57BL/6 J mice (n = 55), combined with preregistered multimodal magnetic resonance imaging with graph-theoretical analyses, we identify structural and network-level correlates of three behavioral phenotypes. Resilient animals exhibited greater microstructural complexity in prefrontal regions, and showed signatures consistent with enhanced inhibitory gating within amygdalar circuits. In contrast, susceptible animals-defined behaviorally by fear generalization and resistance to extinction-exhibited dentate gyrus alterations across all measures, suggesting diminished microstructural adaptability. A third phenotype, impaired threat learning-mice that failed to avoid individuals from a threatening strain-was associated with altered CA1/CA2 microstructure and reduced structural connectivity in pons, pointing to disrupted hippocampal-brainstem interactions during memory consolidation. These findings demonstrate that resilience, susceptibility, and impaired threat learning arise from dissociable patterns of brain organization, with resilience reflecting adaptive circuit-level organization and susceptibility and impaired threat learning exhibiting distinct forms of microstructural and network reorganization.

title: ATF4 Modulates Group 1 mGluR-Dependent molecular signaling, hippocampal plasticity and behavior
abstract: Group 1 metabotropic glutamate receptors (Gp1 mGluRs) are critical effectors in behavior. Abnormal Gp1 mGluR signaling is frequently observed in neurodevelopmental and cognitive disorders. It is established that activation of Gp1 mGluR elicits translation-dependent neuronal plasticity mechanisms, such as long-term synaptic depression (LTD). However, whether and how transcription is involved is not clear. In this study, we study a cellular stress associated transcription factor, activation transcription factor 4 (ATF4). We first employed RNA sequencing and revealed that knocking down ATF4 using ATF4 heterozygous mice upregulates or downregulates multiple genes with known functions in translational control or synaptic plasticity in a sex-dependent manner. When searching for a crosstalk between ATF4 and known synaptic plasticity mechanisms, we found that activation of Gp1 mGluR promotes the expression and nuclear distribution of ATF4. Using ATF4 heterozygous mice, we further confirmed that ATF4 is required for Gp1 mGluR-induced activation of extracellular signal-regulated kinases 1 and 2 (ERK1/2) and phosphorylation of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E (eIF4E), de novo translation and hippocampal LTD at Schaffer-collateral synapses. When assessing animal behavior, our results indicated that knocking down ATF4 impairs learning behavior and precludes mGluR-dependent reduction in repetitive behavior only in female mice. Altogether, our study suggests ATF4 as an activity-dependent transcription factor required for Gp1 mGluR-dependent translation, hippocampal LTD, and behavior.

title: Investigating the associations between neurodevelopmental and psychiatric genetic liability and adverse social and functional outcomes across childhood, adolescence and young-adulthood
abstract: Neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions often originate in youth and can lead to adverse social and functional outcomes. It is unclear whether these associations are driven by genetic liability to these conditions, with possible developmental differences. We examined multivariable associations between polygenic scores (PGS) for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, depression, anxiety and three outcomes: peer problems, educational attainment/employment and suicidality, in childhood, adolescence and young-adulthood. Data were analysed from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children; outcomes at ages 10-13, 16 and 24-25 years. ADHD PGS was associated with peer problems (OR = 1.13, p = 0.020; OR = 1.21, p < 0.0001; OR = 1.14, p = 0.010) and lower educational attainment/employment in childhood, adolescence and young-adulthood(OR = 1.40, p < 0.0001; OR = 1.62, p < 0.0001; OR = 1.29, p = 0.005 respectively) and suicidality in childhood (OR = 1.13, p = 0.030). ASD PGS was associated with peer problems and suicidality in childhood (OR = 1.24, p < 0.0001; OR = 1.24, p = <0.0001) and greater educational attainment in childhood and adolescence (OR = 0.88, p = 0.004; OR = 0.77, p = 0.007). Depression PGS was associated with peer problems in childhood and young-adulthood (OR = 1.18, p = 0.003; OR = 1.21, p < 0.0001), and poorer educational attainment/employment and suicidality in adolescence (OR = 1.39, p = 0.004; OR = 1.28, p < 0.0001) and young-adulthood (OR = 1.26, p = 0.017; OR = 1.42, p < 0.0001). We did not find strong evidence of associations for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder or anxiety PGS. These findings suggest that genetic liability to neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions are associated with a range of social/functional outcomes, although the strength and direction of association vary by PGS, outcome and development stage. This highlights the importance of examining genetic liability to multiple conditions simultaneously and of a developmental perspective.

title: Ketamine Alters Tuning of Neural and Behavioral Spatial Working Memory Precision
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Working memory (WM) is a key element of cognition that depends on accurate internal representation of stimuli and often impaired in psychiatric disorders, including schizophrenia. Prior human neuropharmacological studies with ketamine suggest that glutamate N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs) are critical for spatial WM (sWM), with NMDAR antagonism attenuating task-evoked neural activation and reducing WM accuracy. Animal studies, at the cellular level, and cortical microcircuit models hypothesize that NMDAR antagonism impairs sWM by decreasing the specificity of neuronal responses to spatial locations through broadened spatial tuning. Testing the relevance of this mechanism in humans remains a vital gap in our understanding of sWM and is critical for designing better treatments for WM impairments.

METHODS: To overcome the challenges of measuring neuronal responses invasively in humans, we combined pharmacological manipulation and computational fMRI to show that ketamine broadens neural spatial tuning in healthy adults (N=40). Specifically, we modeled population neuron-level representations, rather than traditionally examined changes in blood oxygen level dependent (BOLD) activation.

RESULTS: Broader neural tuning across visual perception and WM networks was linked to poorer sWM performance under ketamine, implicating tuning changes in sWM deficits. Furthermore, ketamine-induced changes in tuning, compared to the overall magnitude of BOLD activation, were more consistent across individuals and brain regions, suggesting a collective effect of ketamine on neural tuning across spatially-selective regions.

CONCLUSIONS: These findings provide the first empirical evidence linking altered neuronal tuning to NMDAR antagonism and sWM impairments in humans, advancing a mechanistic understanding of glutamatergic mechanisms underlying sWM and related deficits in neuropsychiatric disorders.

title: TMS-Evoked Cortical Reactivity Signatures as a Multidimensional Biomarker of Depression: A TMS-EEG Meta-Analysis from Diagnosis to Prognosis
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Transcranial magnetic stimulation combined with electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) enables perturbation-based assessment of cortical reactivity and has emerged as a promising tool for identifying neurophysiological biomarkers in major depressive disorder (MDD). However, the literature remains fragmented, and TMS-EEG metrics have yet to be systematically integrated within a unified framework spanning diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis.

METHODS: PubMed, Scopus, Ovid, and Web of Science were systematically searched for studies reporting single-pulse TMS-EEG measures in MDD. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed to synthesize evidence across three hierarchical biomarker validation domains: characterization (diagnostic discrimination and state-related symptom tracking), treatment response (intervention monitoring and clinical coupling with remission), and baseline prediction.

RESULTS: Across 21 studies comprising 1,025 patients with MDD and 517 healthy controls, negative-polarity components were significantly enhanced in MDD (Hedges' g = 0.36), driven primarily by the N100 (g = 0.35), which was also associated with greater symptom severity (g = 0.67). Treatment attenuated N100 (g = -0.21) while elevating P180 (g = 0.52). Critically, treatment-induced reduction in negative-polarity responses was strongly coupled with clinical remission (g = 0.91), with the N100 showing the most robust component-level effect (g = 0.85). Preliminary evidence further indicated that baseline negative-polarity components predicted treatment response (g = 1.35).

CONCLUSIONS: TMS-EEG cortical reactivity signatures, particularly negative-polarity components and their N100 subcomponent, demonstrated convergent effects across disease characterization, treatment monitoring, and outcome prediction, supporting their candidacy as multidimensional neurophysiological biomarkers for MDD with potential clinical utility in biomarker-guided precision psychiatry.

title: Inhibitory control and error processing in Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: A mega-analysis of task-based fMRI data by the ENIGMA-OCD consortium
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a chronic condition in which impaired inhibitory control and excessive error monitoring may contribute to maintenance of obsessions and compulsions. This mega-analysis investigates neural activation during response inhibition and error processing using adult (OCD=563; control=348) and child (OCD=83, control=114) data from the ENIGMA-OCD consortium and the ABCD study (probable OCD=343; control=361).

METHODS: Individual participant data was uniformly processed using HALFpipe to extract statistical maps for response inhibition and error processing contrasts. Bayesian multilevel models were used to assess regional and whole-brain effects of OCD, and to examine the association between the OCD clinical profile and task-related activation.

RESULTS: Across inhibitory control tasks, both OCD and control participants showed robust activation in regions implicated in response inhibition and error processing. During response inhibition, compared to controls, adults with OCD showed stronger somatomotor cortex activation, while children with OCD showed stronger occipital cortex activation. Children with probable OCD from the ABCD cohort showed weaker activity in the frontoparietal network in the anterior insula/frontal operculum region. During error processing, relative to controls, adults with OCD showed weaker activation in fronto-striatal regions, while children with OCD showed stronger activation in frontoparietal and attention networks. Greater OCD symptom severity was associated with weaker task-related activation in adults and stronger activation in children during response inhibition.

CONCLUSION: Case-control differences in brain activation during inhibitory control varied by age group and task contrast. Symptom severity emerged as the main clinical correlate of activation during inhibition, suggesting that inhibitory control deficits in OCD may be both state-dependent and developmentally specific.

title: Connection-Level Multi-Omics Reveals Cerebellar-Cortical Dysconnectivity and Divergent Molecular Signatures Across Major Psychiatric Disorders
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Understanding how disease-related connectome alterations relate to underlying molecular systems remains a major challenge in psychiatric disorders.

METHODS: Here we introduce BrainNetAnno (https://brainnetanno.readthedocs.io/en/latest), an open-source framework for molecular annotation of brain network connections that extends multi-omics mapping from regional nodes to inter-regional edges. We applied this framework to resting-state functional connectivity data from a discovery cohort of 2,453 participants and an independent validation cohort of 442, including individuals with major depressive disorder, schizophrenia, generalized anxiety disorder, autism spectrum disorder, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, and healthy controls.

RESULTS: Our analyses revealed a shared transdiagnostic abnormal connectivity pattern (STACP), characterized by cerebellar-cortical dysconnectivity, alongside distinct disorder-specific connectivity deviations (DSCDs) that exhibited structured inter-disorder relationships, including opposition, partial alignment, and near-orthogonality. These connectivity patterns were differentially associated with molecular systems, with mitochondrial phenotypes linked to the STACP and selected DSCDs, and neurotransmitter receptor/transporter profiles primarily associated with DSCDs.

CONCLUSIONS: These findings establish a robust, connection-level framework for linking large-scale connectome abnormalities to multi-omics molecular systems in psychiatric disorders.

title: Quantifying the health and financial burden of adverse childhood experiences in Wales, England and English regions in 2023: a pooled analysis of 10 population surveys
abstract:
Abstract Objectives To update estimates of the health and financial burden of adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) in England and Wales and generate estimates for English regions. Design Population attributable fractions (PAFs) for ACEs were calculated for risks and causes of ill-health using data from 10 randomly stratified cross-sectional ACE studies. PAFs were applied to disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) for England, Wales and English regions for 2023, with financial costs estimated using UK statistical life year values (societal willingness to pay). Setting Households in England and Wales. Participants 28 449 residents aged ≥18 years. Outcome measures PAFs for ACE exposure categories (1 ACE, 2–3 ACEs and ≥4 ACEs) for four health risks (smoking, high alcohol use, drug use and high body mass index (BMI)) and seven causes of ill health (violence, mental illness, cancer, type 2 diabetes, heart disease, respiratory disease and stroke). Annual estimated DALYs and financial costs attributable to ACEs. Results Relative risks for all outcomes increased with ACEs, with risk ratios for ≥4 ACEs ranging from 1.063 (95% CI 1.000 to 1.129, p=0.048) for high BMI to 9.147 (95% CI 7.062 to 11.847, p<0.001) for drug use. For health risks, PAFs for ACEs were highest for drug use (Wales 60.3% and England 56.7%), while ACE-attributable costs were highest for smoking (Wales £1.8 billion and England £22.7 billion). For causes of ill health, PAFs for ACEs were highest for violence (Wales 49.2% and England 46.2%), and costs were highest for mental illness (Wales £1.8 billion and England £37.8 billion). Across all outcomes (accounting for duplication by excluding DALYs for causes linked to the four health risks), total ACE-attributable costs were £7.8 billion for Wales and £115.6 billion for England; costs for English regions ranged from £6.3 billion (North East England) to £18.0 billion (South East England). Conclusions Findings highlight the substantial financial burden of ACEs across England and Wales and provide important information to inform regional activity. There is an urgent and economically justified need for action to prevent ACEs and support those affected by them to reduce the health and economic burden of poor-quality childhoods.

STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THIS STUDY This study uses additional and more recent adverse childhood experience (ACE) studies to update existing estimates of the health and financial burden of ACEs in England and Wales using an increased sample size. Additional analyses now provide estimates of the health and financial burden of ACEs across different English regions, allowing more local interpretation and application of findings. Financial costs were estimated using established statistical life-years approaches, which are based on societal willingness to pay for reductions in the risk of ill health and mortality and therefore include intangible costs. ACE data were retrospectively reported and therefore may be affected by recall bias, while general household surveys are also likely to exclude some of those who have experienced the greatest harm related to ACEs (eg, homelessness, incarceration or premature death). We used cross-sectional data and therefore cannot infer causality; thus, our estimates reflect the health and financial burden associated with, but not definitively wholly attributable to, ACEs. Introduction Exposure to chronic stress in childhood can disrupt children’s developing neurological and physiological systems and embed vulnerability to poorer health and well-being. 1 2 Accordingly, a large body of research has identified how adverse childhood experiences (ACEs), such as child maltreatment, witnessing domestic violence and household member substance misuse, increase the risks of poorer health across the life course. 3 4 ACEs show dose-responsive relationships with both behavioural risk factors for ill health, such as tobacco, alcohol and drug use, 5 6 and major causes of ill health, such as mental illness, cancer and respiratory and cardiovascular diseases. 7 – 9 Such effects mean the health and associated financial costs of ACEs are substantial. For example, annual costs attributable to ACEs for leading health risks and causes in North America and Europe have been estimated to be equivalent to around 3% of each geography’s gross domestic product (GDP). 10 Similar estimates across 28 European nations found costs equivalent to between 1% and 6% of national GDP. 11 In England and Wales, a study using data from the 2017 Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study estimated the annual health costs attributable to ACEs at £42.8 billion (£40.6 billion in England and £2.2 billion in Wales). 12 The study combined data from five general population ACE studies in England and Wales and, in line with other estimates, used a human capital approach to value the health burden of ACEs, based on the cost of lost productivity due to people being removed from the labour force through morbidity or premature mortality. However, the health and social impacts of ACEs affect far more than economic productivity. Thus, an alternative method of valuing the burden of ACEs is through statistical life methods, which focus on the social value of—or society’s willingness to pay for—small reductions in the risk of mortality. 13 14 A recent study using this approach in the USA estimated the annual economic burden of adult health conditions attributable to ACEs at US$13.9 trillion, substantially higher than equivalent estimates using GDP per capita. 15 Understanding the financial burden of ACEs is imperative for informing early intervention and response systems and assessing the potential economic gains of preventing ACEs for future generations. Since 2017, major events such as the COVID-19 pandemic and the rising costs of living linked to global conflict have affected population health, with studies identifying ACEs as a vulnerability for greater harm. 16 – 19 Here, we update estimates of the costs of ACEs in England and Wales using a statistical life methods approach, data from five further ACE studies and data from the 2023 GBD. We also, for the first time, provide estimates of ACE-attributable costs for the nine administrative regions that make up England. Methods Primary data sources Data from 10 cross-sectional ACE studies conducted across various national or local geographies in England and Wales were combined. These included the five studies used in previous cost estimates (conducted 2012–2017) 20 – 24 and five further studies conducted between 2020 and 2024. 16 19 25 26 The initial five studies were restricted to adults aged 18–69 years, while the five further studies were extended to include all adults. Summary details of the 10 studies are provided in online supplemental table S1 . 7 studies were face-to-face household studies, one of which included the option for participants to complete the survey online. All household studies used stratified random sampling approaches with lower super output areas (LSOAs; small geographical areas with a mean population of 1500) as the sampling unit, stratified by region (as appropriate to each study) and deprivation quintile (assigned using the English 27 or Welsh 28 Indices of Multiple Deprivation (IMD)). In five household studies, letters were sent to randomly selected households in sampled LSOAs in advance of an interviewer visit, providing study information and the opportunity to opt out (and a link to the online survey for the one study including this option). For the two other household studies, households in sampled LSOAs were randomly selected by interviewers, and study information was provided at the door. Interviews were conducted by a professional market research company using computer-assisted personal interviewing, with participants able to self-complete sensitive questions (eg, those on ACEs). Participation was voluntary, and informed consent was obtained from all participants. Only one resident per selected household was able to participate. The remaining three studies included two conducted by telephone and online (due to their implementation during the COVID-19 pandemic, when face-to-face interviewing was not appropriate) and one conducted wholly online. The telephone surveys used stratified sampling methodologies, with landline and mobile telephone contacts obtained from a commercial sample provider. Telephone interviews were conducted by a professional market research company. An online survey was incorporated into these studies using a commercial online panel (individuals who are compensated for participating in online research) due to difficulty accessing younger adults by telephone. The online panels were extended to all age groups proportionate to each study area’s population demographics. The final study also used a commercial online panel with participation targeted to represent national demographics. Total study sample sizes and participation rates are shown in online supplemental table S1 . For analysis, data were restricted to individuals with complete ACE and demographic data, with a final sample of 28 449. Demographic data included sex, age group, ethnicity (self-assigned using UK census categories) and deprivation quintile (based on the most recent Welsh or English IMD for each study at the time of data collection). In all studies, data were collected on nine ACEs occurring before the age of 18 years using the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention short ACE tool. 29 The nine ACEs were physical abuse, sexual abuse, verbal abuse, parental separation, exposure to domestic violence, household member alcohol abuse, drug abuse, mental illness and incarceration. In the five latter surveys, the three questions used to measure three types of sexual abuse were replaced with a single question measuring any sexual abuse. Positive responses to ACE questions were summed and categorised into an ACE count category: 0 ACEs, 1 ACE, 2–3 ACEs and ≥4 ACEs. Questions used to measure ACEs and the health outcomes included in this study are shown in online supplemental table S2 , along with variation in questions between studies. All studies provided data on smoking (people who smoke); nine on violence (victimisation in the past year); seven on whether respondents had ever been diagnosed with cancer, type 2 diabetes or respiratory disease; six on drug use (ever used heroin or crack cocaine) and four on high alcohol use (see below), high body mass index (BMI, ≥25.0 kg/m 2 ) and whether participants had ever been diagnosed with heart disease (coronary heart disease/heart attack) or stroke (see online supplemental table S3 ). Our previous estimates included three mental illness outcomes of depression, anxiety and other mental illness based on data from a single study. None of the five newer studies had collected these outcomes separately, but four included a single question asking whether respondents had ever been diagnosed with depression, anxiety or other mental illness. Thus, here we use any mental illness as an outcome, including data from all studies that measured mental illness (n=5). While none of the newer studies contributed data on alcohol use, we amended our classification of high alcohol use consistent with methodological changes in the measurement of alcohol use as a risk factor in the GBD study. Thus, high alcohol use was determined based on estimated consumption above the theoretical minimum risk exposure level for Western Europe by age and gender 30 (see online supplemental table S2 ). Calculating population attributable fraction Statistical analysis was undertaken in IBM SPSS V.24, and data editing and calculations were performed in Excel. Risk ratios (RRs) and 95% CIs associated with each ACE count level for each outcome were calculated using log-binomial models, 31 controlling for study (ie, study ID), study method (face-to-face, telephone or online), sex, age group, deprivation quintile of residence and ethnicity (white or other than white). Population attributable fractions (PAFs) were generated separately for England and Wales using equivalent ACE prevalence levels (raw proportions based on individual participant analysis from the combined dataset; see Results). Consistent with previous estimates, 12 PAF values were calculated at each ACE count level (1 ACE vs 0 ACEs; 2–3 ACEs vs 0 ACEs; ≥4 ACEs vs 0 ACEs) according to: P A F A C E α = P A C E α × ( R R A C E α − 1 ) ( P A C E 0 ) + ( P A C E 1 × R R A C E 1 ) + ( P A C E 2 − 3 × R R A C E 2 − 3 ) + ( P A C E ≥ 4 × R R A C E ≥ 4 ) where α is the ACE count category for the PAF being calculated, RR ACE is the pooled RR associated with each ACE count and P ACE is the proportion of the sample exposed to each ACE count. Overall PAFs for ACEs were calculated by summing the three PAF values. 32 Calculating ACE-attributable costs Health outcomes were matched to risk factor and cause categories in the 2023 GBD study 33 (eg, mental illness was matched to the GBD category for mental disorders; see online supplemental table S4 ). Disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) estimates for 2023 for each matched category for Wales, England and each English region were extracted and summed for age categories 15–49 years, 50–69 years and ≥70 years. PAFs were applied to DALYs for each risk factor and cause to estimate the number of DALYs attributable to ACEs by ACE level. Costs were then calculated by valuing each DALY at £70 000, the latest government-published estimate of UK willingness to pay per quality-adjusted life year. 34 This value is based on research estimating how much people would be willing to pay to mitigate risks of injury and premature death and consequently represents an intangible cost. To provide a level of comparison with previous estimates, 12 ACE costs for England and Wales were also calculated using the previous human capital-based method of valuing DALYs, where each DALY was valued at each region’s GVA (gross value added) per capita. To estimate total ACE-attributable costs across all included risk factors and causes of ill health, we excluded DALYs for risk factors related to included causes of ill health (eg, those for smoking related to cancer). Sensitivity analyses for Wales and England estimates were run using the upper and lower bounds (uncertainty intervals) for DALYs, generating PAFs using the upper and lower CIs for RRs and restricting all data to people aged 15–69 years. Patient and public involvement Patients and the public were not involved in the design or planning of the study.
